Resident records are stored in a locked cabinet in the office, or in a secure electronic system at one central location with individual passwords. Records are not left in common areas, vehicles or open on screens.
Cash and current financial information for residents are kept locked, and only staff trained under RTS-05 have access.
Staff are given access only to records they need to do their job. The Administrator reviews electronic access at least quarterly and removes access on the day a staff member leaves.

Staff share information only with persons authorized by law or by a signed authorization, and then only the minimum necessary. Disclosures to treating providers, the Waiver Support Coordinator and APD for operations, payment and oversight follow HIPAA.
At admission, the Program Director gives each resident and legal representative the Notice of Privacy Practices, explains it in an accessible way, and files a signed acknowledgment.
Staff do not discuss residents' information in front of other residents, visitors or in public places, and do not share information on social media or in text messages that are not secure.
Staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's bedroom or bathroom, except in an emergency, and supervise in the least intrusive way consistent with safety.

When APD or State of Florida staff ask for records, the Monitoring Custodian verifies identification, provides access, and provides a complete copy as soon as possible and no later than 2 calendar days after the request, in line with GOV-07.
The agency retains a copy of each record for 6 years in accordance with HIPAA. Records are destroyed only after that period, by shredding or secure electronic deletion, and the destruction is logged.

Before any use of a resident's name, image or information for fundraising or publicity, staff obtain the written consent described in RTS-10. Staff do not post photographs or personal stories without it.

Staff report any suspected privacy breach, such as a lost record, a misdirected message or unauthorized access, to the Privacy Officer within 24 hours. The Privacy Officer investigates, limits the harm, notifies the resident or representative, and makes required notices under HIPAA.

Residents and representatives may request to see and get a copy of the resident's record, ask for corrections and ask for a list of disclosures. The Privacy Officer responds in writing within the time required by HIPAA.
The Privacy Officer audits privacy practices at least twice a year and reports results to QI under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Designates the Privacy Officer, secures records storage and ensures staff training.
Handles access requests, breaches, authorizations and audits.
Provides records to APD and State of Florida staff on request within required time frames.
Protect information, share only what is authorized, respect physical privacy and report breaches.

documentation: Signed confidentiality agreements
Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgments
Authorizations to release information
Disclosure log
Breach reports and notifications
Record destruction log
Access reviews and audit reports

policies.title: Personal Funds, Personal Needs Allowance and Property Management
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Program Director, all staff who handle resident funds or property
policies.purpose: To protect residents' money and belongings, make sure residents receive their personal needs allowance, and keep accurate records of funds and property.
policies.policy: Resident funds belong to the resident. Neither the licensee nor any staff member may gain financial benefit by charging fees against, borrowing, or using a resident's funds (Rule 65G-2.009(4)(a), F.A.C.). Each resident keeps a personal needs allowance of at least 18% of the SSI federal benefit rate, which is $178.92 per month at the 2026 SSI rate of $994 (Rule 65G-2.018, F.A.C.). The APD room-and-board standard is $583.42 per month, and room and board is claimed on Form 65G-13.008A within 90 days after month end (Rule 65G-13.008, F.A.C.). If [AGENCY NAME] manages a resident's funds, it does so only with written authorization renewed every year and with the accounting, receipts and safeguards below. Where the agency or a staff member is the SSA representative payee, it also follows 20 CFR 416.610. A property inventory is completed on admission and kept current.

definitions.definition: The monthly amount, at least 18% of the SSI federal benefit rate, that the resident keeps for personal use.
The monthly payment toward housing and food. The APD standard is $583.42 per month.
A person or organization appointed by the Social Security Administration to manage a beneficiary's benefits.
Mixing a resident's funds with funds of the agency, staff or anyone other than other residents.
A written, itemized list of a resident's belongings, signed by the licensee and the resident or representative.

procedures: At admission, the Administrator determines with the resident, legal representative and Waiver Support Coordinator who will manage the resident's funds, and documents the decision. The resident manages their own funds unless they choose assistance or the team and representative decide otherwise.

If [AGENCY NAME] will manage funds, the Program Director obtains a written authorization signed by the resident or legal representative, and obtains a new one every year. Funds are not accepted without it.
The Administrator trains every staff member with access to resident funds on these procedures before they handle any funds, and documents the training (Rule 65G-2.009(4)(b)).

The Administrator ensures each resident receives the PNA of at least $178.92 per month (2026 SSI rate of $994, at 18%). It is given or credited to the resident's account before any other deduction and is never withheld as a consequence.

Where benefits are received, the agency maintains a checking or savings account for resident funds. Resident funds are never commingled with the funds of the agency, staff or anyone other than other residents (Rule 65G-2.009(4)(f)-(g)).
Cash for each resident is accounted for on a separate form and kept locked. Cash and current financial information are secured on the premises (Rule 65G-2.009(4)(h)).
For every deposit or withdrawal, staff record the date, amount, purpose and staff name and signature. For withdrawals the resident uses at their own discretion, the resident also signs.
Staff obtain a written receipt for each purchase of $25.00 or more and keep it for at least one year.

At least monthly, the Program Director prepares a monthly accounting for each resident listing the balance, each deposit and withdrawal and its purpose. The Program Director reconciles the available amount to the most recent ending balance, signs the reconciliation and sends it to the Administrator for review.

The Administrator reviews the monthly accounting and spot checks receipts and cash counts at least quarterly. Any discrepancy is investigated at once, the resident or representative is informed, and the missing funds are restored. Suspected exploitation is reported under BSP-03.

No staff member or the licensee may borrow a resident's money, use it for their own benefit, or be named beneficiary of a resident's life insurance unless related to the resident by blood or marriage (Rule 65G-2.009(4)(j)).

The Administrator collects room and board in line with the residency agreement and APD standards. The agency submits the room-and-board claim on Form 65G-13.008A within 90 days after the end of the month and records the submission date.

Where an agency representative serves as representative payee, the Administrator follows Social Security Administration rules in 20 CFR 416.610, keeps the beneficiary's funds separate from agency funds and gives the required annual accounting to the Social Security Administration.

Within 30 days of admission, the licensee and the resident or representative complete and sign an itemized property inventory of the resident's belongings. A copy is given to the resident or representative and one is filed in the record.
The Program Director updates the inventory within 30 days of the resident acquiring or losing any item, at least every 12 months, and 30 days before discharge. Each update is signed.

At discharge or transfer, the Program Director returns all funds, accounts, and property listed on the inventory to the resident or representative, obtains a signed receipt, and files the final accounting in the record under PCS-05.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures PNA is paid, approves authorizations, reviews accountings quarterly, files room-and-board claims and prevents misuse of funds.
Maintains authorizations, monthly accountings, reconciliations and property inventories.
Complete training, record every transaction, obtain receipts and keep funds secure.
Authorize fund management, review accountings and sign inventories.

documentation: Annual written authorization for fund management
Staff training record on funds procedures
Monthly accounting and reconciliation for each resident
Cash accounting forms and receipts for purchases of $25.00 or more (kept at least one year)
PNA payment records
Form 65G-13.008A submissions with dates
Signed property inventories and updates
Quarterly review notes

policies.title: Informed Consent and Decision-Making Support
policies.applies_to: All residents, guardians, guardian advocates and authorized representatives; the Facility Operator/Program Director, Registered Nurse/nursing oversight, direct support professionals (DSPs) and any staff who obtain or rely on consent.
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's right to consent to or refuse treatment is respected, that decisions are made by the right person with the right supports, and that written consent is obtained and kept in the record before services, treatments, monitoring or interventions that require it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] recognizes that every person with a developmental disability has the right to consent to or refuse treatment, subject to the authority of a guardian advocate (s. 393.12, F.S.) or guardian (ch. 744, F.S.) where one has been appointed (s. 393.13, F.S.; Rule 65G-2.009(1)(b)8, F.A.C.). Each resident is presumed able to make their own decisions unless a court has ruled otherwise. The agency provides supports so residents can understand and take part in decisions, and it never treats a lack of a guardian or a refusal as a reason to retaliate or discharge. The agency records each resident's guardianship status, legal competency and authorized representatives (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)6). It obtains written authorization for routine medical and dental care (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)4), written consent before video monitoring (Rule 65G-2.009(7)(b)3), consent information for any reactive strategy (Rule 65G-8.003(1)), and consent for medication administered by unlicensed staff under s. 393.506, F.S. No behavioral program is implemented unless it has been reviewed as required under APD rule (s. 393.13, F.S.).

definitions.definition: Permission given voluntarily by the resident or the legally authorized decision-maker after receiving understandable information about the proposal, its purpose, risks, benefits, alternatives and the right to refuse or withdraw.
A person appointed by a court under ch. 744, F.S. (guardian) or s. 393.12, F.S. (guardian advocate) to make specified decisions for a person who has been found unable to make them.
A person the resident has chosen, or who is otherwise legally authorized, to receive information and help with decisions, as recorded in the resident's record.
Assistance such as plain-language explanation, visual aids, more time, a trusted person present, or the Waiver Support Coordinator's help so the resident can make or take part in a decision.
An emergency technique governed by Ch. 65G-8, F.A.C., used to protect a person from imminent harm, for which consent information must be kept in the record.

procedures: At admission, the Facility Operator/Program Director (or designee) asks the Waiver Support Coordinator and the resident for court orders and documents showing any guardianship, guardian advocate or other authorized representative, and copies them to the resident record.

Within the same admission process, the designee records in the record the resident's guardianship status, legal competency and authorized representatives, and notes which decisions each person may make (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)6).

If no guardian exists, staff treat the resident as the decision-maker for themselves. Staff do not ask family members to consent unless the resident has chosen them as a supporter or they hold legal authority.

Before asking for any consent, the staff member explains the matter in plain language and in the resident's preferred communication method (see RTS-07), allows enough time, and offers a trusted person to be present.

Staff document the explanation given, the supports used, and the resident's response. If the resident appears not to understand, staff stop, try another approach and tell the Program Director, who involves the Waiver Support Coordinator and legal representative as needed.

Before routine medical or dental care is provided, the nurse or designee obtains written authorization from the resident or legal decision-maker and files it in the record (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)4). Follow-up of medical appointments is handled under HLT-02.

For medication administered or supervised by unlicensed DSPs under s. 393.506, F.S., the nurse or Program Director obtains the required consent from the resident or legal decision-maker before staff begin, and files it in the record. The Program Director confirms the current consent requirements with APD when forms are reviewed each year.
Before any video monitoring begins, the Program Director obtains written consent from the resident or guardian/legal representative and explains when and where monitoring occurs (see RTS-09).

Before any behavior plan is implemented, the Program Director confirms it has been reviewed as required by APD rule and that consent is on file. Before any reactive strategy may be used, consent information required by Rule 65G-8.003(1) is placed in the record (see BSP-01 and BSP-02).

If a resident refuses a treatment, medication or service, staff respect the refusal, never force or coerce, document the refusal, and notify the nurse and Program Director the same shift. The nurse assesses the health risk and informs the physician as needed (see HLT-04).

If the refusal creates an immediate health or safety risk, staff follow HLT-04 and call 911. Staff do not treat an emergency as permission to override a competent person's decisions beyond what law allows.

If a guardian or guardian advocate refuses or withdraws consent, staff follow the decision unless it would result in abuse or neglect. In that case the Program Director consults the Waiver Support Coordinator, APD and, if required, reports under BSP-03.

When a resident's capacity appears to change, or a decision-maker is unreachable, the Program Director notifies the Waiver Support Coordinator and support team and documents efforts to reach the person. The agency does not accept informal or verbal consent where written consent is required.

The Program Director reviews each resident's consent file at admission, at each support plan meeting and at least annually, and renews or replaces forms that are expired or no longer reflect the resident's wishes.

Within 30 days of learning of any new information about guardianship or decision-making authority, staff update the record (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)) and tell all staff who need to know on a need-to-know basis (see RTS-04).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and when a resident's decision-making arrangements change (see STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Obtain and file guardianship documents and consents; make sure no service starts without required consent; resolve disputes with the Waiver Support Coordinator and APD.
Obtain medical, dental and medication consent; explain health information in understandable terms; assess risk when a resident refuses treatment.
Provide decision-making supports, respect refusals, and document and report refusals and any signs the resident does not understand.
Assist with guardianship questions and support-plan decisions; agency staff cooperate and share information as permitted.

documentation: Court orders and records of guardianship, guardian advocate and authorized representative status in the resident record
Signed written authorization for routine medical and dental care
Signed consent for video monitoring, medication administration by unlicensed staff and reactive strategies
Notes on supports used and the resident's decision or refusal
Annual consent review checklist

policies.title: Nondiscrimination and Communication Access
policies.applies_to: All residents, applicants, guardians and family members; all staff and anyone acting for [AGENCY NAME].
federal: Title VI, Civil Rights Act (45 CFR 80)
policies.purpose: To make sure no one is excluded from services, denied benefits or treated differently because of disability or any other protected characteristic, and that residents, guardians and others can communicate effectively with staff and receive information in a form they can use.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not discriminate on the basis of disability, race, color, national origin, sex, age, religion or any other protected characteristic. Residents may not be excluded or denied benefits because of a developmental disability (Rule 65G-2.009(1)(b)9, F.A.C.; s. 393.13, F.S.). The agency makes sure DSPs can communicate effectively with residents, support coordinators, APD staff and families (Rule 65G-2.008(3)(a)). Before admission it confirms it can meet each person's programmatic and physical accessibility needs (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(d)). Interpreters, translated materials and alternate formats are provided at no cost to the resident or family, including language access for guardians.

definitions.definition: Communication that lets the person understand and express themselves, using the aids, services or supports needed.

A tool or service that supports communication, such as a qualified interpreter, sign language, picture boards, large print, plain-language or easy-read documents, assistive technology, or a speech-generating device.
A limited ability to read, speak, write or understand English that requires language assistance.
A change to a rule, practice, space or service that lets a person with a disability have equal access.

procedures: At referral and admission, the Program Director asks the resident, guardian and Waiver Support Coordinator about each person's preferred language, communication method, hearing, vision, literacy and any communication device, and records the answers in the record.

Before accepting a referral, the Program Director reviews whether the home can meet the person's programmatic and physical accessibility needs (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(d)) and documents the review. A referral is never refused merely because the person has a disability or needs communication supports.

The Program Director adds each resident's communication profile (how they express yes/no, pain, distress, choices) to the support plan and the daily staff guide so every DSP knows it (see PCS-02, PCS-03).

Before hiring, the Program Director verifies that a DSP candidate can communicate effectively with residents, support coordinators, APD staff and families (Rule 65G-2.008(3)(a)); communication skills are assessed at the interview and at the performance evaluation (see STF-03).

Staff use the resident's communication method at all times and keep devices charged, working and within reach. If a device fails, staff tell the Program Director the same shift and use an alternate method until it is repaired (see HLT-07).

When a qualified interpreter or translation is needed for a resident, guardian or family member, the Program Director arranges it at no cost. Staff do not use residents or minor family members as interpreters except in an emergency until an interpreter is reached.

Notices, house rules, the grievance procedure, rights information, consent forms and the abuse reporting number (1-800-962-2873) are provided in plain language, and in the person's language or another accessible format on request, and are explained verbally.

A resident or guardian who needs a document or meeting in another format, or a change to a rule or routine because of a disability, tells any staff member. The staff member tells the Program Director, who decides within 5 business days in consultation with the resident and Waiver Support Coordinator and records the decision.
If an accommodation cannot be provided, the Program Director explains why in writing, offers an alternative that works for the person, and tells the person how to file a grievance (see RTS-03).
Residents are offered the same meals, activities, outings, rooms and privileges as others in the home, subject only to individualized, documented support plan decisions made under RTS-02.

Staff must not use slurs, mocking, threats or demeaning language about a resident's disability, race, language or other characteristic. Violations are reported to the Program Director and handled under STF-07 and BSP-03.

Any person who believes they were discriminated against may report it to any staff member, the Program Director at [PHONE], or externally. The Program Director logs and investigates every report as a grievance and prohibits retaliation.

The Program Director reviews communication access at each annual support plan review and during quality reviews, including interpreter requests, accommodation requests and any complaints (see GOV-04).
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually, including how to use each resident's communication supports (see STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Ensure nondiscrimination, arrange interpreters and accessible formats, decide accommodation requests, and review accessibility before admission.
Communicate effectively with each resident using their preferred method, maintain devices, and report barriers or discriminatory conduct.
Make sure health information is given in a form the resident can understand.

documentation: Communication profile for each resident in the record
Pre-admission accessibility review
Requests for interpreters, translations and accommodations and the agency's response
Language assistance and interpreter logs
Grievances alleging discrimination and the outcome

policies.title: House Rules, Resident Government and Community Activities
policies.applies_to: All residents and staff of the group home, and anyone who helps develop or enforce house rules or plans resident activities.
policies.purpose: To make sure the home's rules are written, developed with residents and available to them, that residents have a meaningful voice in how the home runs, and that residents can take part in community life based on their own choices.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] establishes written house rules, developed in consultation with residents, and makes them available to residents and employees (Rule 65G-2.009(1)(d), F.A.C.). House rules may not conflict with the Bill of Rights (s. 393.13, F.S.) or with HCBS settings requirements, and any limit on an individual right is handled only under RTS-02. The agency helps residents establish a resident government when appropriate (Rule 65G-2.009(1)(e); s. 393.13). The agency provides opportunities to participate in community activities (Rule 65G-2.009(2)) and encourages public transportation where it is available and appropriate (Rule 65G-2.009(14)(o)).

definitions.definition: The written expectations for living together in the home, such as quiet hours, chores, shared spaces and visitors, that apply to everyone and are not individual restrictions.
A resident-led group or meeting in which residents raise concerns, suggest changes and take part in decisions about the home, with support from staff as the residents choose.
An activity outside the home in the general community, chosen by the resident, such as recreation, worship, volunteering, shopping, classes or social events.

procedures: Within 30 days of opening and before the first admission, the Program Director drafts proposed house rules limited to what is needed for safety and group living, and reviews them with the residents already living in the home.

Residents are consulted by meeting, one-on-one conversation or the means the resident prefers, with communication supports (see RTS-07). The Program Director records who was consulted, what was suggested and what changed (Rule 65G-2.009(1)(d)).

The final house rules are written in plain language, with pictures or other formats as needed, and posted in a common area and given to each resident, guardian and employee at admission or when updated.
Staff review the house rules with each new resident at admission and explain them. New employees receive and sign for them at orientation.

The Program Director checks house rules before adoption and annually to make sure they do not restrict access to food at any time, visitors, privacy, use of the resident's own room, personal funds, or movement. Any rule that does is revised, and individual restrictions are handled only under RTS-02.
Staff apply house rules equally to all residents. Staff may not use house rules as punishment, to take away rights or to discipline residents.
The Program Director offers residents the opportunity to form a resident government within 60 days of opening and after each new admission, and records whether the residents wish to participate.

If residents choose to organize, the Program Director arranges a place and time for resident meetings at least monthly, provides communication supports, and a staff member takes notes only as the residents ask.

The Program Director responds in writing to resident suggestions, requests and concerns raised at resident meetings within 14 days, and records what action was taken or why not. Unresolved concerns are treated as grievances (see RTS-03).

During the person-centered planning process, the Waiver Support Coordinator and staff ask each resident what community activities they want to do, how often and with whom, and these preferences are written into the support plan and implementation plan (see PCS-02, PCS-03, PCS-04).

The Program Director and staff offer each resident opportunities to take part in community activities regularly and record the opportunities offered, what was chosen and any refusal. Activities are not limited to group outings arranged only for staff convenience.

Where public transportation is available and appropriate for a resident, staff teach and encourage its use, consistent with the resident's safety needs and support plan (Rule 65G-2.009(14)(o)); vehicle transport follows ENV-06.
Staffing is scheduled so residents can leave the home for chosen activities (see STF-01), and the Program Director reports barriers that prevent access to the Facility Operator and addresses them.
The Program Director reviews house rules, resident meeting notes and community activity records at least annually and as part of the quality review (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Develop house rules with residents, make them available, support resident government, and make sure community activity opportunities are offered and documented.
Explain and fairly apply the rules, support residents to attend resident meetings and community activities, and record participation.
May take part in developing house rules, join or lead resident government, and choose activities and refuse them.

documentation: Written house rules with the date of resident consultation and revisions
Signed receipt of house rules by employees; resident acknowledgment where the resident chooses
Resident meeting notes and the agency's written responses
Community activity log showing opportunities offered, activities chosen and refusals
Annual review of house rules

policies.title: Video Monitoring and Surveillance
policies.applies_to: All residents, guardians and legal representatives; Facility Operator/Program Director, staff and any vendor with access to video equipment or footage at the home.
policies.purpose: To make sure any video monitoring at the home protects residents without violating their privacy or dignity, is used only with written consent and written protocols, and that footage is preserved and shared as Florida rules require.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] may use video cameras only as permitted by Rule 65G-2.009(7), F.A.C. Footage may not be used to humiliate, punish, demean or violate a resident's privacy (Rule 65G-2.009(7)(a)). Before video is used, the agency has written criteria for which residents are monitored and written protocols for who may access footage, the purpose of monitoring, and how, when and where footage is stored (minimum 30-day retention). Written consent is obtained from the resident, or the guardian or legal representative, before use, and the person is told when and where monitoring occurs. Remote interactive monitoring is limited to vocational and educational settings, medical or special treatment spaces, administrative offices and common areas, and is never used in bedrooms or bathrooms (Rule 65G-2.009(7)(c)). The agency does not install bedroom cameras without a variance granted by APD. Video is a facility record available to APD, and inadequate storage is not a defense. APD may restrict or suspend video monitoring (Rule 65G-2.009(7)(d)-(f)).

definitions.definition: The use of cameras that record or transmit images of residents or the home.
Live viewing, or the ability to view or communicate, from a location outside the room being monitored.
An event involving serious injury, death, abuse, neglect, exploitation, elopement or other serious harm that requires reporting under BSP-04 or other agency policy.
The ability of a person who is not physically at the home to view or retrieve live or recorded footage.

procedures: The Program Director decides whether the home will use video monitoring at all. If it will not, no camera is installed and no consent is requested. If it will, the Facility Operator approves the plan in writing before any camera is installed.

The Program Director writes the criteria for which residents are monitored and why, and the written protocols covering who may access footage, the purpose of the monitoring, and how, when and where footage is stored, with a minimum 30-day retention period (Rule 65G-2.009(7)).

Cameras may be placed only in common areas and other spaces allowed under Rule 65G-2.009(7)(c). Cameras are never placed in bedrooms or bathrooms. A bedroom camera may be considered only if APD has granted a variance for that resident and location; the Program Director keeps the approved variance order on file before installing.

Before video is used for a resident, the Program Director explains in plain language, with communication supports (see RTS-07), when and where monitoring occurs, who can view footage and why, and obtains written consent from the resident, or the guardian or legal representative (see RTS-06). The resident's refusal is respected, and no admission or services depend on consent.
Signs or notices telling residents, staff and visitors that cameras are in use are posted in the monitored areas.

The Program Director provides APD with the titles and positions of everyone with off-site access to footage, and updates APD when those people change. Off-site access is protected with firewalls or equivalent safeguards and individual passwords. Access lists are reviewed quarterly.
Only people named in the written protocol may view footage, and only for the documented purpose. Each access to recorded footage is logged with name, date, time and reason.

Staff must never use footage, screenshots or recordings to humiliate, punish, demean or share on social media or personal devices. Violations are reported to the Program Director and handled under STF-07 and BSP-03.
Footage is stored on a secured device or system and kept for at least 30 days. The Program Director verifies storage capacity monthly so retention is not shortened by lack of space.

The Program Director immediately preserves footage, and stops it from being overwritten, in four situations: for 30 days as a general rule; after any critical incident captured on video; on notice of a law enforcement or DCF investigation; and on APD's request.

When an incident occurs, the Program Director identifies relevant cameras within 1 hour of learning of it, exports and saves the footage to a protected location, and records the date, time and person who preserved it (see BSP-04).

Footage is a facility record, available to APD. The Program Director provides requested footage to APD promptly, and inadequate storage is never given as an excuse. Disclosure to others is controlled under RTS-04.
If APD restricts or suspends video monitoring, the Program Director stops monitoring as directed, documents the date and notifies affected residents and guardians.
A resident or guardian may withdraw consent at any time. The Program Director then stops monitoring that resident and records the withdrawal the same day.
The Program Director reviews video monitoring each year, including who is monitored, consents, access lists, storage and any variance orders, and corrects deficiencies (see GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve any use of video monitoring and ensure resources are available for storage and security.
Maintain written criteria and protocols, obtain consent, manage access, notify APD of off-site access, preserve footage and respond to APD requests.
Report camera concerns and misuse; never access, copy or share footage unless named in the protocol.

documentation: Written criteria and protocols for video monitoring
Signed consent from the resident, guardian or legal representative, and any withdrawal
List of titles and positions with off-site access, as provided to APD
Access log for recorded footage
Footage preservation records for incidents, investigations and APD requests
Variance order, if any
Annual review of video monitoring

policies.title: Use of Resident Name, Image and Information; Solicitation
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, board members, contractors and anyone who uses resident names, images or information for fundraising, marketing, websites, social media or public communications on behalf of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To protect residents from having their name, image, voice, personal information or disability used to raise money or promote the agency without proper written permission, and to keep that permission on file.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] obtains written permission from the resident, if competent, or from the legal representative before using the resident's image, voice, name, picture, personal information or disability to secure donations (Rule 65G-2.009(10), F.A.C.). The same consent standard applies to marketing materials, websites and social media. Permission is voluntary, specific and revocable, and is never a condition of admission or services. Written releases are kept in the individual's record. Marketing uses of protected health information also require a valid authorization under 45 CFR 164.508.

definitions.definition: A request for donations, gifts, sponsorship or other financial support.
Brochures, websites, social media posts, videos, newsletters, presentations and other items that promote the agency.
A signed written permission naming what may be used, how, where, by whom and for how long.
A guardian, guardian advocate or other person with legal authority to make the decision for the resident.

procedures: No staff member, volunteer or contractor may use a resident's image, voice, name, picture, personal information or disability for donations, marketing or public communications unless the Program Director confirms a valid written release is on file.

Before asking for permission, the Program Director determines who may consent: the resident, if competent, or the legal representative (see RTS-06). Consent is not requested from family members who lack legal authority.

The Program Director explains, in plain language and using the resident's communication supports (see RTS-07), what would be used, where it would appear, who would see it, how long it would be used and that the resident may say no or withdraw at any time without any effect on services.

The release is in writing and names the specific items to be used (for example, photo, first name only, story), the specific purposes (fundraising, website, social media, print), the period of use and the person's right to revoke it. Blanket or open-ended releases are not accepted.
For any marketing use of protected health information, the release also meets HIPAA authorization requirements (45 CFR 164.508) and is reviewed under RTS-04.
The signed release is filed in the individual's record and a copy is given to the person who signed it.

Before any content is published or sent, the Program Director checks the release against the content, confirms that no identifying detail (such as home address, diagnoses or full name) goes beyond what was authorized, and approves it in writing.
Staff may not post pictures, videos or stories about residents on personal social media accounts or personal devices at any time, with or without permission.

Staff may not solicit money, gifts or loans from residents, guardians or families for themselves or any other person, and may not use a resident's disability or situation to ask the public for donations without a release. Violations are handled under STF-07.

When a resident or legal representative revokes permission, the Program Director removes the person's name, image and information from active websites, social media and materials within 5 business days and records it. The agency does not recall printed items already distributed, but does not reuse them.
Photos or video taken for a resident's personal use, such as with friends and family, are the resident's property and are not agency marketing material (see RTS-05).
The Program Director reviews marketing materials, websites and social media pages at least every 6 months to check that all uses of residents match current releases.

The Program Director reports any unauthorized use of resident information to the Facility Operator the same day, removes it, notifies the resident or representative and handles it as a privacy matter under RTS-04.
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation (see STF-04).

responsibilities.duty: Approve all uses of resident images and information, obtain and file releases, and remove content when permission ends.
Not use or share resident information, images or stories without a verified release, and not use personal accounts or devices for resident content.
May give, limit or withdraw permission at any time without consequence.

documentation: Signed releases in the individual's record
Revocation records and removal dates
Approval records for published content
Six-month review of websites and marketing
Incident records of unauthorized use

policies.title: Referral, Admission and Transition In
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, nursing staff, DSPs and anyone who receives referrals, screens applicants or helps a new resident move in.
policies.purpose: To make sure people are admitted only when the home matches their needs and its license, that APD and the Waiver Support Coordinator are involved, and that each person moves in safely, with choice and with their records, property and supports in place.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written admission and termination criteria, which are also part of the license application (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(a), F.A.C.). The home serves only persons with developmental disabilities, whether or not they are APD clients (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(b)), and serves only residents whose characteristics match the license (Rule 65G-2.006(3)). The agency notifies APD before accepting each new resident (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(c)). It does not accept a person unless it can meet the person's programmatic and physical accessibility needs and the placement will not harm current residents (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(d)-(e)). Admissions come through Waiver Support Coordinator referrals and APD regional crisis placements, and services begin only after an authorization. The agency does not exceed licensed capacity, and census changes are reported as required.

definitions.definition: Written conditions that describe who the home can serve, based on the license, the home's staffing and physical setup, and the needs of current residents.
The level of care, age, sex and other characteristics on the license application that APD approved for the home.
The person who coordinates the resident's iBudget services and support plan.
The approval to provide and bill the waiver service, shown on the resident's cost plan.
A written plan with safeguards for a resident whose history presents a risk to self or others, reviewed before admission under Rule 65G-2.009(9)(c)2.
A written list of the resident's belongings completed at placement.

procedures: The Program Director keeps written admission and termination criteria consistent with the license application and reviews them annually and whenever the license or capacity changes (see GOV-03, GOV-06).

All referrals are received from the Waiver Support Coordinator or an APD regional office, including crisis placements. The Program Director logs the date, source and basic information for every referral, whether accepted or declined.

Before accepting a person, the Program Director confirms: the person has a developmental disability; the person's characteristics (level of care, age, sex) match the license application; and a bed is available within licensed capacity (Rule 65G-2.006(3); Rule 65G-2.009(3)(b)).
If a placement would deviate from the characteristics on the license application, the Program Director gets APD approval before any placement and keeps the approval in the file.

If the person is not an APD client, the Program Director obtains and provides to APD documentation of the developmental disability under Ch. 65G-4, along with medical needs, behavioral issues and any known criminal history.

The Program Director and nurse review the person's assessments, support plan, medical and medication information, behavior plan, communication needs and any Safety Plan before accepting. Any Safety Plan is reviewed before admission (Rule 65G-2.009(9)(c)2) and its safeguards are put in place first (see BSP-07).

The Program Director confirms the home can meet the person's programmatic and physical accessibility needs and that the placement will not harm current residents' safety or services, considering the other residents' needs, staffing and supervision (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(d)-(e)). The reasons for accepting or declining are documented. Disability alone is not a reason to decline (see RTS-07).
The Program Director verifies the waiver authorization and the rate level with the Waiver Support Coordinator, and does not start services or billing until the authorization is in place (see GOV-05).
The Program Director notifies APD in writing before accepting each new resident (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(c)), using the method the Regional Office requires.

If the home is receiving its first resident, the Program Director also notifies the local zoning authority as required for community residential homes (s. 419.001, F.S.). The date and name of the person notified are recorded.

Before placement, the person and their representative are offered a visit to the home, to meet housemates and staff and to see the bedroom, and the agency cooperates with the Waiver Support Coordinator in planning the move (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(j)). The person's choice about the move is respected and documented.

Before the move, the Program Director briefs all staff who will work with the person on the person's needs, communication methods, supports, medications, risks and preferences, and the nurse reviews health needs and medication orders (see PCS-06, HLT-02).

On the day of the move, staff and the resident complete the property inventory, including clothing, personal items and valuables, and both sign it, with a copy to the resident or representative (Rule 65G-2.009(3)(j)).

Within the first 2 days, staff review the Bill of Rights, grievance process, house rules, abuse reporting number and privacy practices with the resident and representative in an understandable manner, and collect consents and authorizations (see RTS-01, RTS-03, RTS-04, RTS-06, RTS-08).
Within 5 calendar days of the admission, the Program Director sends APD the census change report in writing (Rule 65G-2.009(3); Rule 65G-2.006(2)) and records the date sent.
The Program Director sets up the individual record with the required contents and updates it within 30 days of any new information (Rule 65G-2.009(5)) (see REC-01).

The agency participates in the person-centered support plan process with the Waiver Support Coordinator and monitors the first 30 days closely, with the Program Director checking in with the resident and representative about how the move is going (see PCS-02, PCS-03).

responsibilities.duty: Apply admission criteria, confirm license match and capacity, notify APD and zoning, coordinate the move, and ensure the census report is filed within 5 calendar days.
Review medical and medication information before admission and prepare health supports.
Welcome the resident, complete the property inventory, and follow the briefing and support plan.
Make the referral, confirm authorization and coordinate the support plan; the agency cooperates fully.

documentation: Written admission and termination criteria
Referral log with acceptance or decline reasons
APD pre-admission notice and any approval for deviation from license characteristics
Documentation of developmental disability and history for non-APD clients
Safety Plan review record, if applicable
Authorization verification
Visit and transition record
Property inventory signed at placement
Census change report to APD
Zoning notification for the first resident

policies.title: Person-Centered Planning and Support Plan Coordination with the Waiver Support Coordinator
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, Residential Habilitation direct support staff, and the licensed nurse or other health professional consulted by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident's services are planned around the resident's own goals, preferences and needs. The plan comes from the person-centered process led by the Waiver Support Coordinator (WSC). [AGENCY NAME] coordinates with the WSC so the resident's current support plan is in the record and guides daily care.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides individualized care that reflects each resident's personal goals, abilities, sex, age and special needs. We keep the current support plan supplied by the resident's WSC in the resident record. We facilitate implementation of support plans, behavior plans and directions from medical professionals. We work with the WSC and the resident's legal representative or authorized representative, and we take part in staff training and meetings that APD requires. Any limit on a resident's rights or choices must be supported by a documented person-centered justification and must not be imposed as a facility convenience.

definitions.definition: The person-centered plan for the resident, developed through the iBudget process and supplied to [AGENCY NAME] by the Waiver Support Coordinator.
The person who coordinates the resident's iBudget waiver services and supports and who is the provider's main link to the resident's planning team.
[AGENCY NAME]'s written plan, developed with the resident, describing how Residential Habilitation supports will help the resident meet support plan goals. See PCS-03.
A guardian, guardian advocate or other person with legal authority to act for the resident.

procedures: Before or on the day of admission, the Program Director asks the resident's WSC for the current support plan, any cost plan, and any behavior plan or medical directions. The Program Director records the date of each request.

The Program Director confirms the support plan is the current version. If the plan is missing or out of date, the Program Director documents the request to the WSC and follows up in writing until it is received.
The Program Director places the current support plan in the resident record in the location required for resident records, and replaces superseded plans within 30 days of receiving the updated plan.

Within 5 business days of receiving the plan or an update, the Program Director reads it, notes the goals, preferences, support needs, supervision level and Residential Habilitation level, and briefs all direct support staff, who initial a staff acknowledgment sheet.

The Program Director meets with the resident, and with the legal representative where there is one, to ask what matters to the resident: daily routine, food, privacy, relationships, activities, work and community goals. The Program Director records this in the resident's person-centered profile.
Staff provide care that reflects the resident's goals, abilities, sex, age and special needs. Supports are not applied as a one-size-fits-all house routine.
The Program Director develops the implementation plan with the resident, tied to the support plan goals, as described in PCS-03.

The Program Director invites the WSC, the resident and the legal representative to any [AGENCY NAME] meeting held to review the resident's services, and attends planning meetings, annual plan meetings and any team meetings the WSC schedules.

Staff carry out the support plan, behavior plan and directions from medical professionals. If staff believe a direction cannot be followed or is not working, they tell the Program Director the same day. The Program Director then contacts the WSC or the prescriber and documents the contact.

When a resident needs medical or dental care, the Program Director or designee contacts the WSC as needed so care is timely. If no WSC is assigned, the Program Director contacts the resident's legal representative and documents the contact.

If a person-centered review suggests a modification to a resident's rights or settings, such as limits on access to food, visitors, privacy or a lockable bedroom door, the Program Director does not impose it. The Program Director follows RTS-01 and RTS-02, and the modification may be used only with a documented person-centered justification.

The Program Director notifies the WSC promptly of significant changes in the resident's needs, health, behavior, preferences or circumstances that may require the support plan to be revised, and records the notice and the WSC's response.
The Program Director or designee participates in staff training and meetings that APD requires, and keeps the sign-in sheets and training notices.

The Program Director reviews each resident's record at least quarterly, along with the quarterly summary in PCS-03, to confirm the support plan in the file is current and that services match it. Findings are recorded and corrective steps taken.
Concerns about plan content raised by the resident or legal representative are sent to the WSC without delay and are also handled under RTS-03 if the person wishes to file a grievance.

responsibilities.duty: Obtains and files the current support plan, briefs staff, attends planning meetings, communicates with the WSC, and ensures care follows the plan.
Know each resident's support plan goals, deliver individualized supports, report concerns or changes, and attend required training and meetings.
Advises on health-related plan elements and medical directions (see HLT-02).
Leads the support plan process and supplies the current plan to [AGENCY NAME].

documentation: Current support plan in the resident record
Log of requests to and communications with the WSC
Staff acknowledgment sheets for plan briefings
Person-centered profile and meeting notes
Records of notices to the WSC about changes
Training and meeting attendance records

policies.title: Implementation of Supports, Implementation Plan and Daily Documentation
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director and all direct support staff providing Residential Habilitation
policies.purpose: To make sure supports are delivered as planned and documented every day. Each resident has an implementation plan, and progress is reported to the Waiver Support Coordinator in quarterly summaries and an annual report.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] writes an implementation plan for each resident, developed with the resident and tied to support plan goals. We carry out the plan, document services daily, and file quarterly summaries and an annual report with the Waiver Support Coordinator. Resident records are kept current and updated within 30 days of receiving new information. All documentation is in legible English. We follow through on health care appointments and train staff on any changes in medication, diet, positioning or equipment.

definitions.definition: The written plan, developed with the resident, stating how Residential Habilitation supports will be provided to meet support plan goals.
A written summary of services provided and the resident's progress toward goals, filed with the WSC each quarter.
A written yearly report on services and progress, filed with the WSC.
Entries made by staff each day showing the supports delivered and the resident's status.

procedures: Within 30 days of admission, the Program Director meets with the resident, and with the legal representative where there is one, to develop the implementation plan. This is an agency internal deadline and does not replace any shorter time APD or the WSC requires.

The implementation plan lists each support plan goal, the specific supports staff will provide, who provides them, how often, how progress will be measured, and the resident's own words about how they want supports provided.

The resident, and the legal representative where applicable, review and sign the plan or the record notes why a signature was not obtained. The Program Director gives the resident a copy in an accessible format (see RTS-07).
The Program Director files the implementation plan, and any behavior plan, in the resident record, and sends a copy to the WSC.
The Program Director trains staff on each resident's implementation plan and behavior plan before the staff member works alone with that resident. Staff sign a training acknowledgment.

Staff provide supports as written and document them each shift in the daily record. Each entry states the date, time, staff name or initials, the supports given, the resident's response, and any incident, refusal or change.
Staff write legibly in English. Errors are corrected by a single line, initial and date, never by erasure or correction fluid. Electronic entries record the author and date automatically.
Any medical or behavioral incident or physician/therapist order that could affect health or safety is also entered in the shift communication record under PCS-06.
The Program Director reviews daily documentation at least weekly for completeness and consistency with the plan. Gaps are corrected with the staff member and recorded.

Within the quarter, the Program Director prepares a quarterly summary for each resident covering services provided, progress on each goal, health and behavior events, community activities, and recommended changes. The summary is filed with the WSC and a copy kept in the record.
Once a year, and in time for the annual support plan meeting, the Program Director prepares the annual report and files it with the WSC. A copy is kept in the record.

The Program Director updates the record within 30 days of receiving any new information, including new orders, evaluations, plans or contacts. If required information is unavailable, the Program Director documents the diligent efforts made to get it, including dates and persons contacted.
When a health care appointment is held, staff record the visit and any orders or recommendations, schedule any follow-up, and tell the Program Director the same day if the visit results in a change.

When there is a change in medication, diet, positioning or equipment, the Program Director or the licensed nurse trains all staff on the change before the next shift they work and records the training. See HLT-01, HLT-03 and HLT-07.
If supports cannot be provided as planned, staff document the reason immediately and notify the Program Director, who informs the WSC where the plan needs to change.
The Program Director audits each record at least quarterly, and results feed into GOV-04 quality improvement.

responsibilities.duty: Develops implementation plans with residents, files quarterly summaries and annual reports, audits documentation and keeps records current.
Deliver supports as planned, write legible daily documentation each shift, and report changes.
Receives the implementation plan, quarterly summaries and annual report.

documentation: Signed implementation plan for each resident
Behavior plan, where one exists
Daily documentation and shift records
Quarterly summaries and annual reports with filing dates
Staff training acknowledgments on plans and changes
Record audit forms
Records of diligent efforts to obtain unavailable information

policies.title: Community Integration and Employment Choice
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director and all direct support staff
policies.purpose: To make sure residents live as full members of the community: taking part in community activities, recreation and social life, and having real choices about work. This reflects the Florida Bill of Rights and the federal HCBS settings requirements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides residents opportunities for community activities and supports social interaction, exercise and recreation. Residents are never required to perform work for the facility, and the facility does not depend on resident labor. Chores may only be encouraged, not required. Incidental transportation is provided as a typical household would provide it. We support each resident's choice to seek competitive integrated employment, in coordination with the WSC.

definitions.definition: Full access to the greater community, including opportunities to seek employment, engage in community life, control personal resources and receive services in the community, to the same degree as people not receiving Medicaid HCBS.
Work in the community, paid at or above minimum wage, alongside people without disabilities, as the person chooses.
Transportation provided as part of ordinary household life, such as rides to shops, appointments or activities, the way a typical household would provide it.

procedures: At admission and at least annually, the Program Director asks each resident about their interests, preferred activities, faith and cultural practices, friends and family, community places and work goals, and records the answers in the person-centered profile.

The Program Director builds each resident's preferences into the implementation plan (PCS-03) and the weekly activity schedule so that community activities are offered at least weekly, in addition to any day program.

Staff offer community activities outside the home, such as shopping, dining, faith services, recreation, volunteering, clubs and visits with family and friends. Offers and the resident's responses, including refusals, are documented.
Staff support each resident's exercise and recreation of choice, and document participation.
Activities are individual, not only group outings. Staff do not require residents to join group activities, and the resident's decline is respected.

Staff provide or arrange incidental transportation as a typical household would, using vehicles and drivers that meet ENV-06. Transportation limits that stop a resident from taking part in community life are brought to the Program Director.

The Program Director confirms that no resident is required to do chores or labor for the facility. Staff may encourage a resident to take part in household tasks, and the resident's choice to take part or not is recorded and respected. The facility does not rely on resident labor to meet staffing or operating needs.
Any work a resident chooses to do is documented as the resident's own choice, and where paid, wages are the resident's property and are handled under RTS-05.

The Program Director asks each working-age resident, at least annually, whether they want to work or explore work, and records the answer. Information about competitive integrated employment is shared in a form the resident understands.

If a resident wants to explore employment, the Program Director informs the WSC and asks for a referral to employment services, and supports the resident to attend assessments, interviews, training and job activities. Staff schedules are adjusted as feasible.
Staff support the resident to follow up on employment plans, and the Program Director records progress.
Staff support residents to keep in touch with family, friends and community contacts, including visits at times the resident chooses, consistent with RTS-01.
If a resident's access to the community or visitors is limited for any reason, the Program Director follows RTS-02. No limit is imposed without a documented person-centered justification.
The Program Director reviews community activity and employment-choice records quarterly, includes them in the quarterly summary, and addresses residents who have few community opportunities.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures community activities and employment choice are offered, arranges transportation, and prohibits required resident labor.
Offer and support community activities, encourage but never require chores, and document offers and participation.
Coordinates referrals to employment and day services.

documentation: Person-centered profile with interests and work goals
Weekly activity schedule and activity log, including refusals
Record of annual employment-choice conversation
Referral communications with WSC
Quarterly summary entries on community integration

policies.title: Transfer, Discharge and Termination of Services
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, administrative staff and direct support staff
policies.purpose: To make sure a resident is transferred, discharged or terminated only for proper reasons, with proper notice, planning and protection of the resident's rights, belongings and records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] follows termination procedures consistent with APD's termination rules (Chapter 65G-3, F.A.C.). Before any transfer, we discuss the transfer and the reasons with the resident, authorized representative, support coordinator, APD and other service providers. On discharge we return all personal belongings, referencing the property inventory, and the resident's records go with the resident. We report each census change to APD in writing within 5 calendar days.

definitions.definition: A resident's move to another residence, including to another facility run by the same licensee.
The ending of [AGENCY NAME]'s provision of residential services to a resident.
Any change in the number of residents in the facility, such as an admission, discharge, transfer or death.
The written list of the resident's personal belongings, kept current in the resident record.

procedures: The Program Director must not start a discharge or termination until the reasons have been reviewed against APD's termination rules and the admission and termination criteria in the facility's written policies. The Facility Operator approves the decision in writing.

If a resident's needs no longer match the facility's licensed capacity or resident characteristics (see GOV-06), the Program Director notifies the WSC and APD promptly and works with the team to find a suitable setting. The resident is not left without a safe place to go.

The Program Director informs the resident and the authorized representative of the proposed action, the reasons, and the resident's right to appeal, in plain language and an accessible format. The notice states how to request a Medicaid fair hearing, consistent with 42 CFR 431.210-.244, and how to contact the WSC and APD.

Before any transfer, the Program Director discusses the transfer and its reasons with the resident, the authorized representative, the WSC, APD and other service providers, and records each discussion with date and persons.
The Program Director supports the resident to visit and choose the new home where possible, and asks the resident about preferences for the move.

If the licensee operates more than one facility, the Program Director obtains APD's approval before transferring a resident between them, except in an emergency. Emergency transfers are reported to APD immediately and the reason is documented.

The Program Director arranges for the nurse or a medication-trained staff member to prepare a transition summary: current medications and supply, orders, allergies, diet, equipment, behavior plan, health care contacts and appointments.

Staff update the property inventory 30 days before a planned discharge, and again on the day of discharge. The resident or representative signs to confirm that all personal belongings, funds and medications are returned. Any difference is documented.
The Program Director returns the resident's personal funds with a final accounting under RTS-05, and obtains a signed receipt.
The resident's records go with the resident. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a copy of the record for 6 years from discharge and stores it securely under REC-01 and RTS-04.
The Program Director reports the census change in writing to APD within 5 calendar days of the transfer, discharge or termination, and notifies the WSC and any other agencies in the same period.
The Program Director sends the information required for billing and enrollment updates to the person responsible for GOV-05 so that no services are billed after the resident leaves.

If a resident is transferred as an emergency to a hospital or crisis setting, staff follow HLT-04, notify the representative and WSC, and do not discharge the resident without a planned process. Belongings are secured.
For any discharge, the Program Director completes a discharge summary within 10 calendar days, including the reason, the resident's destination, who was notified and when, and any follow-up.
The Program Director reviews each discharge in the quality improvement process (GOV-04) to find ways to avoid avoidable discharges.

responsibilities.duty: Approves discharge or termination decisions and obtains APD approval for inter-facility transfers.
Gives notice, coordinates the transfer, returns belongings and funds, reports census changes within 5 calendar days and retains records.
Assist with packing, inventory and a safe, respectful move.
Prepare medication and health transition information.

documentation: Notice of proposed transfer or discharge, including appeal rights
Records of discussions with resident, representative, WSC, APD and providers
APD approval for inter-facility transfer
Property inventory and signed return of belongings
Final funds accounting and receipt
Transition summary
Written census change report to APD with date sent
Discharge summary
Retained copy of the record (6 years)

policies.title: Staff Communication and Shift Handoff
policies.applies_to: All direct support staff, the Program Director and the licensed nurse
policies.purpose: To make sure that staff on each shift know about recent incidents and any information that could affect residents' health or safety, so that care is consistent across shifts.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a system to communicate recent incidents and resident information to staff on later shifts. The system includes written documentation of medical or behavioral incidents and physician or therapist orders that could affect health or safety, and a procedure to make sure the information is reviewed by staff on all shifts. Communication documentation is kept for at least one year after each entry and is available to APD during inspections.

definitions.definition: The written or electronic log in which staff record incidents, orders and resident information for oncoming shifts.
The exchange of information between outgoing and oncoming staff at a shift change.
An event involving a resident's health, injury, illness, behavior or safety that later staff need to know about.

procedures: The Program Director designates a single shift communication record, paper or electronic, for the home. It is kept in a set location and is available to all staff on duty.
Each entry shows the date, time, resident, the staff member's name, what happened or what was ordered, actions taken, and any follow-up needed by the next shift.
Staff enter medical or behavioral incidents in the record before the end of the shift in which they occur. Reportable incidents are also handled under BSP-04.

Staff enter any physician or therapist order that could affect health or safety, such as medication, diet, positioning, activity or equipment changes, on the day the order is received, with the source and the effective date.

Outgoing and oncoming staff hold a verbal handoff at every shift change, with overlap time. Outgoing staff must not leave until the oncoming staff member has arrived, to avoid leaving residents unattended (see STF-01).
The handoff covers each resident's condition, changes, appointments, medications given or due, behavior events, supervision needs, visitors, any open issues and any urgent follow-up.
Each oncoming staff member reads all entries made since their last shift and signs or initials the record to show review. No staff member begins work with residents without doing this.
The Program Director checks the record at least weekly to confirm that every shift is reviewing entries, and follows up with any staff member who has not signed.
If an urgent safety matter is found, such as a new order or a significant incident, the Program Director or supervisor phones staff not on duty who will work the next shift, and records the call.
Information needed by staff is shared on a need-to-know basis and in line with RTS-04. The record is not left where visitors can see it.
Where the record is electronic, access is by individual login and it can be printed on request for APD.
The record is kept for at least one year after each entry and is made available to APD during inspections. Archived records are stored securely.
The Program Director reviews entries monthly for patterns, such as repeated incidents, and brings them to the quality improvement review in GOV-04.
The Program Director updates new staff on the system during orientation (STF-04) and re-trains staff who do not use it correctly.

responsibilities.duty: Establishes and monitors the system, checks that all shifts review entries, and keeps records at least one year.
Record incidents and orders promptly, give a verbal handoff, and review the record at the start of each shift.
Enters or confirms health-related orders and changes that affect staff practice.

documentation: Shift communication record with staff review initials
Handoff checklists, if used
Weekly Program Director review notes
Archive of entries kept at least one year

policies.title: Medication Administration and Staff Certification
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, direct support staff who administer or assist with medication, and the licensed nurse
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive medication safely, as prescribed, and only from staff who have completed the required Florida training and validation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] gives medication only according to the written order or prescription of the resident's health care practitioner. Prescription medication is kept in its original labeled container and stored in a locked enclosure accessible only to staff. Unlicensed staff administer medication only after completing the APD Basic Medication Administration course and onsite validation, and they keep their validation and annual in-service current. Residents who are able to are encouraged to self-administer. Errors and adverse reactions are reported and acted on immediately.

definitions.definition: Medication Administration Record, the daily record of prescription and non-prescription medication given, kept under Chapter 65G-7, F.A.C.
Onsite observation by an approved validator of a staff member giving medication to an actual resident, using an actual medication, to confirm competence.
Any deviation from the prescriber's order, including wrong resident, drug, dose, route or time, or a missed or omitted dose.
A resident taking their own medication, which may be supervised by trained staff, where the physician has deemed the resident capable.

procedures: Staff give medication only on a written order or prescription from the resident's health care practitioner. The nurse or Program Director verifies and files each new order before the first dose, and enters it on the MAR.

Prescription medication is kept in the original dated pharmacy container showing the prescription number, directions, resident name, physician name and pharmacy address. Staff do not give medication from unlabeled, altered or relabeled containers, or from another resident's supply.

Medication is stored in a locked enclosure accessible only to staff. Keys are held by the staff member on duty. Medications needing refrigeration are stored in a locked container or locked refrigerator, separate from food. Storage areas are checked for temperature and cleanliness as the nurse directs.

If the home holds any controlled substance, it is stored under double lock, counted at every shift change by two staff, and any discrepancy is reported to the Program Director immediately and to law enforcement where required.

Only staff who hold a current APD Basic Medication Administration certificate and current validation may administer medication. The Program Director keeps a current list and does not assign medication duties to anyone else.

Before assigning medication duties, the Program Director confirms the staff member completed the initial course of at least 6 hours given by an agency-approved trainer, passed the exam with at least 85% and 100% on the MAR section, and was validated by an approved validator.

Validation for oral, enteral, ophthalmic, rectal and inhaled routes is done onsite with an actual resident and medication, initially and every year. Otic, transdermal and topical routes are validated by simulation in the initial course.

Each staff member completes the annual update and revalidation, and the annual 2-hour in-service on medication administration and error prevention. The Program Director schedules revalidation within the 60 days before expiry, tracks all due dates on a training tracker, and alerts staff 90 days before expiry.

A staff member who misses revalidation or the annual in-service stops administering medication immediately and must repeat the initial course before administering again. The Program Director reassigns medication duties and documents the date.

Residents whose physician has deemed them capable are encouraged to self-administer. Staff make the medication available and remind the resident, and record this on the MAR. The physician's determination is kept in the record. Staff supervise self-administration only within their training.

Before each administration, staff check the Five Rights (right resident, medication, dose, route and time), compare the label to the MAR, wash hands, and observe the resident take the medication. They record it on the MAR immediately after, never before, giving it.

Staff keep a current, accurate daily record of all prescription and non-prescription medication given or refused, per Chapter 65G-7, F.A.C. Refusals, omissions and PRN reasons and effects are documented, and the prescriber is contacted where the order requires.

Staff report adverse reactions immediately to the prescriber or the facility's licensed medical professional. If neither can be reached, staff seek medical attention immediately, including calling 911 where appropriate, and then notify the Program Director and the legal representative.

Any medication error is reported to the Program Director immediately. Staff contact the prescriber or pharmacist for instructions, monitor the resident, and complete an error report as Chapter 65G-7 requires. The Program Director also notifies the legal representative and WSC.
A hospital admission caused by a medication error is a critical incident and is reported to APD within 4 hours, under BSP-04.

When there is evidence of medication errors, the Program Director retrains the staff member, and the staff member is re-verified before resuming medication duties. Retraining is documented, and repeated errors are handled through STF-03.
The licensed nurse or Program Director reviews MARs at least weekly and audits stock against records monthly. Findings and error trends are reported to the quality improvement review under GOV-04.
Medication needing disposal, such as discontinued or expired medication, is handled and returned or destroyed as the pharmacy or nurse directs, with two staff witnessing and a written record.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures only certified and validated staff give medication, tracks revalidation, ensures secure storage, and reports errors and critical incidents.
Give medication as ordered, document on the MAR, store securely, and report errors and reactions immediately.
Reviews orders and MARs, advises on errors and reactions, and trains staff on medication changes.
Provide orders and guidance following errors or reactions.

documentation: Written orders and prescriptions
Medication Administration Records
Medication error reports and follow-up
Adverse reaction reports
Staff medication certificates, validation records and annual in-service records
Training tracker with revalidation due dates
Controlled substance count logs, if applicable
Physician determination for self-administration
Storage checks, audits and disposal records

policies.title: Nursing Oversight and Health Care Coordination
policies.applies_to: All residents, the Facility Operator/Program Director, direct support professionals (DSPs) and any licensed nurse or other clinician engaged by [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident receives timely, coordinated medical, dental and other health care, and that nursing oversight is used where the law, a physician order, the support plan or the iBudget handbook requires it.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] coordinates every resident's health care, follows up on every health appointment, and uses licensed nursing oversight whenever it is required. Chapter 65G-2, F.A.C., does not require a licensed nurse in a group home, and DSPs who have completed the training and validation required by s. 393.506, F.S., may administer or supervise self-administration of medication. [AGENCY NAME] will nonetheless arrange nursing oversight whenever a resident's support plan, a physician's order or the Medicaid iBudget handbook (Rule 59G-13.070, F.A.C.) calls for it.
