DSPs do not perform tasks that require a licensed nurse unless the task is lawfully permitted for unlicensed staff and staff are trained and validated for it. The agency keeps each resident's physician and dentist information current in the record, follows up on every appointment, and contacts the waiver support coordinator when needed to obtain timely medical and dental care.

definitions.definition: Review, teaching, monitoring or direct services by a licensed nurse, used when required by a physician order, the resident's support plan or the iBudget handbook.
The resident's waiver support coordinator who coordinates the resident's services and supports.
Any medical, dental, therapy, specialist or other health-related visit, in person or by telehealth.
The guardian, guardian advocate or other person legally authorized to make decisions for the resident.

procedures: At admission, the Program Director records in the resident record the name, address and phone number of the resident's physician and dentist, and of any specialists or therapists, and confirms the information with the resident and legal representative.

The Program Director reviews each new resident's support plan, physician orders and any behavior or health protocols at admission to identify every task that requires nursing oversight, and lists those tasks on the resident's health coordination sheet.

If a plan, order or the iBudget handbook requires nursing oversight, the Program Director arranges for a licensed nurse, documents the nurse's name and contact information in the record, and records the frequency and scope of oversight in writing.
The Program Director maintains a calendar of upcoming medical, dental, therapy and specialist appointments for each resident and assigns a DSP to arrange transportation and accompaniment as needed.
Before each appointment, the assigned DSP prepares the resident's current medication list, recent change-of-condition notes, and a list of questions or concerns reported by staff or the resident.
At each appointment, the accompanying DSP brings the appointment follow-up form, asks the provider to give any orders, recommendations or changes in writing, and records them.
On return, the DSP documents the outcome of the appointment on the follow-up form on the same shift and gives it to the Program Director.

The Program Director reviews the form within one business day and takes appropriate action: schedules any follow-up visits, labs, tests or referrals, obtains new or changed orders, and updates medication records.

If the visit results in a changed order, new diet, new equipment or new precaution, the Program Director trains every DSP on the change before the DSP works alone with the resident and documents the training with staff signatures.
The Program Director sends new medication orders or changes to the person responsible for medication administration so the medication record is updated and staff comply with HLT-01.

If a resident cannot get a timely medical or dental appointment, lacks a provider, cannot obtain needed care or equipment, or the health need goes unmet, the Program Director contacts the support coordinator promptly and documents the date, person contacted and result.

The Program Director informs the legal representative of appointment results, medication changes and care recommendations, unless the resident has the right to decide and has chosen otherwise, and documents the communication.

Where a nurse provides oversight, the nurse reports findings and recommendations to the Program Director in writing, and the Program Director records the response and completion date of each recommendation.
The Program Director updates the resident record within 30 days of any new health information received and follows up with the appointment provider if documentation has not been received.
If a resident's health condition changes, staff follow HLT-04 and, where a medication reaction is suspected, HLT-01.

Quarterly, the Program Director audits each resident record to confirm that physician and dentist information is current, appointments have been completed and follow-ups are closed, and reports results under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure health care coordination, nursing oversight where required, appointment follow-up, support coordinator contact and record accuracy.
Attend appointments, obtain written instructions, document outcomes, carry out orders and notify the Program Director of any health concerns.
Perform the oversight, teaching and monitoring specified in the order or plan, and report findings in writing.
Coordinate access to medical and dental care and services when contacted by the agency.

documentation: Physician and dentist names, addresses and phone numbers in the resident record
Health coordination sheet listing tasks that require nursing oversight
Appointment calendar and appointment follow-up forms with outcomes
Written provider orders and recommendations
Staff training records for changes in orders or plans
Nurse oversight reports and responses (when applicable)
Support coordinator contact log
Quarterly record audit results

policies.title: Health Monitoring, Seizures and Choking Risk
policies.applies_to: All residents, DSPs, the Program Director and any clinician who provides health protocols to the home
policies.purpose: To ensure staff monitor each resident's health, know each resident's individual risks for seizures and choking or aspiration, and take immediate and correct emergency action.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies each resident's health risks, records special instructions for carrying, lifting, positioning, bathing and meal assistance in the resident record, and trains every DSP on seizure and aspiration protocols and each resident's individual plan before the DSP works alone. In an emergency, staff take immediate action: they call 911, begin CPR for a person who is not breathing and has no pulse, and give back blows and abdominal thrusts for choking. At least one DSP with current CPR certification is on site whenever residents are present. A life-threatening injury or illness is a critical incident and is reported within 4 hours.

definitions.definition: The written, resident-specific instructions from a physician or clinician describing how staff respond to and document a seizure.
The entry of food, liquid or other material into the airway or lungs.
Blockage of the airway that prevents or severely limits breathing.
An incident defined by APD as requiring initial notice within 4 hours, including a life-threatening injury or illness.

procedures: At admission and at every plan update, the Program Director identifies each resident's health monitoring needs, including seizure disorders, swallowing or choking risk, aspiration risk and any physician-ordered monitoring, from the support plan, physician orders and the support coordinator.
The Program Director records in the resident record special instructions for carrying, lifting, positioning, bathing and meal assistance for each resident who needs them.

The Program Director obtains written seizure and aspiration/choking protocols from the physician or treating clinician for each resident at risk and places them in the resident record and at the location where staff can reach them quickly.

Before working alone with a resident, each DSP is trained on the resident's individual plan, special instructions, seizure and aspiration protocols and emergency steps, and signs the training record; the Program Director or designee verifies understanding by demonstration or review.
Each DSP completes classroom first aid, including the abdominal thrust maneuver, and CPR within 90 days of providing direct services, as described in HLT-06.
The Program Director schedules staff so that at least one DSP with current CPR certification is on site whenever residents are present, and checks certification expiration dates monthly.

During meals, DSPs follow each resident's individual meal assistance, positioning and diet instructions and stay within sight and reach of residents with choking or aspiration risk, as described in ENV-05.

DSPs observe and record changes in each resident's health, such as breathing, alertness, eating and drinking, skin, pain and seizure activity, and report concerns to the Program Director on the same shift.

If a resident has a seizure, the DSP follows the resident's written protocol, notes the time of onset, duration, description and after-effects, protects the resident from injury, and calls 911 when the protocol requires or whenever the seizure presents an emergency.

If a resident is choking, the DSP gives back blows and abdominal thrusts as trained and calls 911 immediately or has another person call, and continues until the object is cleared or emergency responders take over.
If a resident has no pulse and is not breathing, the DSP calls 911 immediately and starts CPR and continues until emergency responders take over.

After any emergency, the DSP stays with the resident, accompanies the resident to the hospital if directed by the Program Director, and brings the resident's face sheet, medication list and protocols.
The DSP or Program Director immediately notifies the legal representative and support coordinator, as described in HLT-04.

If the event is a life-threatening injury or illness, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours and submits the completed APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day, as described in BSP-04.

The Program Director reviews each seizure, choking, aspiration or emergency event within one business day, updates the resident's plan with the physician or support coordinator if needed, and retrains staff on any change.
Annually, and when a resident's condition changes, the Program Director reviews each resident's protocols with the physician and confirms staff training records are current.

responsibilities.duty: Obtain protocols, record special instructions, schedule CPR-certified coverage, train staff and report critical incidents.
Know each resident's risks and plan, monitor health, take immediate emergency action and document events.
Provide written seizure, swallowing and positioning orders and protocols.
Receive notice of health events and help coordinate follow-up care.

documentation: Special instructions for carrying, lifting, positioning, bathing and meal assistance in the resident record
Seizure and aspiration/choking protocols
Staff training records on individual plans and protocols
First aid and CPR certificates and certification tracking
Seizure and health observation logs
Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 and notification log for critical incidents
Post-event review notes

policies.title: Change of Condition and Emergency Medical Care
policies.applies_to: All residents, DSPs, the Program Director and the Facility Operator
policies.purpose: To ensure staff recognize and respond immediately to a change in a resident's condition or a medical emergency, notify the right people and make the required reports to APD.
policies.policy: Staff take immediate action to resolve any emergency, including calling 911, performing CPR and giving abdominal thrusts. They immediately notify the resident's legal representative and support coordinator. Urgent care, emergency room or hospital treatment for injury or sudden-onset illness is a reportable incident due to the APD Regional Office within 1 calendar day; a life-threatening injury or illness is a critical incident requiring initial notice within 4 hours and the completed form within 1 calendar day. Emergency numbers are posted at every phone extension. Staff take immediate action on any report of a possible adverse reaction to medication.

definitions.definition: Any noticeable change in a resident's physical, mental, behavioral or functional status from baseline, including new symptoms, injury, refusal to eat or drink, or a possible medication reaction.
A life-threatening injury or illness or other event requiring APD initial notice within 4 hours.
An incident, including urgent care, ER or hospital treatment for injury or sudden-onset illness, that must be reported to the Regional Office within 1 calendar day.
The APD form used to report critical and reportable incidents.

procedures: The Program Director posts emergency numbers at every phone extension, including 911, doctors, ambulance, Poison Control, the support coordinator and the APD Regional Office, and checks them monthly.
Any DSP who observes a change in condition or receives a report from the resident assesses the resident, stays with the resident and reports to the Program Director or on-call supervisor immediately.

If the resident is in immediate danger, unresponsive, not breathing, choking, having a serious injury, a prolonged seizure or other emergency, the DSP calls 911 first and takes immediate action as trained, including CPR or abdominal thrusts.

If a resident may be having an adverse reaction to a medication, the DSP takes immediate action: stops further doses if directed by the prescriber or Poison Control, calls 911 if there is an emergency, and contacts the prescriber or Poison Control for guidance, as described in HLT-01.
For a non-emergency change in condition, the DSP or Program Director contacts the resident's physician or the nurse overseeing care, follows their instructions and documents them.
The DSP or Program Director immediately notifies the resident's legal representative and the support coordinator of the emergency or change in condition and documents the time and person contacted.
A DSP accompanies the resident to the hospital or urgent care when directed, bringing the face sheet, medication list, physician and insurance information and the resident's relevant protocols.
Another DSP or the on-call supervisor arranges replacement coverage so the remaining residents are supervised, as described in STF-01.

If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected as the cause of an injury or condition, the DSP or Program Director calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately, as described in BSP-03.

The Program Director determines whether the event is a critical incident (life-threatening injury or illness) or a reportable incident (urgent care, ER or hospital treatment for injury or sudden-onset illness).
For a critical incident, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours and submits the completed Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day.
For a reportable incident, the Program Director submits Form OP 3-0006 to the Regional Office within 1 calendar day.
The Program Director submits any follow-up information to APD within 5 days, as required for incident reports.
The DSP documents the event factually in the daily record and incident report before the end of the shift, and the information is passed on at shift handoff under PCS-06.

After the resident returns, the Program Director obtains discharge instructions and new orders, ensures follow-up care and medication changes are carried out under HLT-02, and trains staff on any new precautions.
The Program Director reviews the event within 3 business days to identify causes, whether the plan needs to be updated, and whether staff need retraining, and reports trends under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Recognize changes, call 911, take immediate action, notify the Program Director and document.
Notify the legal representative and support coordinator, report incidents to APD within required timeframes, arrange follow-up and post emergency numbers.
Ensure staffing and resources to respond to emergencies and review incident trends.
Receive immediate notification and assist with follow-up services.

documentation: Emergency phone number postings (verified monthly)
Daily notes and change-of-condition documentation
APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 with 4-hour notification log (critical incidents) and follow-up submissions
Notification log for legal representative, support coordinator and physician
Hospital/urgent care discharge instructions and new orders
Post-event review notes

policies.title: Death of an Individual
policies.applies_to: All residents, DSPs, the Program Director and the Facility Operator
policies.purpose: To ensure the death of a resident is handled with dignity, that required notifications and reports are made on time, and that evidence and records are preserved.
policies.policy: When a resident dies, staff call 911 and begin emergency response unless the person is clearly deceased and resuscitation is not required by the resident's documented wishes. [AGENCY NAME] immediately notifies the legal representative and support coordinator and gives the APD Regional Office initial notice of an unexpected death within 4 hours of becoming aware of it, with the completed Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day. A death that is not unexpected is a reportable incident due within 1 calendar day. If abuse, neglect or exploitation is suspected, staff call the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately. Personal belongings are returned using the property inventory, the census change is reported to APD within 5 calendar days, and records, video footage and medication records are preserved.

definitions.definition: A death that was not anticipated based on the resident's known medical condition and prognosis, treated as a critical incident.
A death that was anticipated based on a known terminal or advanced illness, reported as a reportable incident.
The written list of a resident's personal belongings maintained in the record.

procedures: The DSP who finds a resident unresponsive or not breathing calls 911 immediately and begins CPR unless a valid, documented order or directive on file says otherwise, and continues until emergency responders take over.
The DSP notifies the Program Director or on-call supervisor immediately, who comes to the home or directs on-site staff as needed.
Staff secure the area, keep other residents supervised and supported, and avoid disturbing the scene beyond what is necessary for emergency care until responders or law enforcement say otherwise.
If there is any reason to suspect abuse, neglect or exploitation, the DSP or Program Director calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately and follows BSP-03.
The Program Director immediately notifies the legal representative and the support coordinator, by telephone, and documents the time and person contacted.
The Program Director determines whether the death was unexpected or not unexpected, in consultation with the physician or nurse when needed, and documents the basis.

For an unexpected death, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours of becoming aware, by phone, e-mail or APD's reporting system, and records the time and method.

The Program Director submits the completed APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 to the Regional Office within 1 calendar day for an unexpected death, and submits it within 1 calendar day for a death that is not unexpected, and submits any follow-up information within 5 days.

The Program Director preserves the resident's record, any video footage covering the critical incident, and the medication administration records and medication supply, and does not alter or delete them.
The Program Director cooperates with law enforcement, the medical examiner, APD, DCF and any other investigating authority and provides requested records.

The Program Director follows the legal representative's and family's direction on notifying other family members, clergy and funeral arrangements, and supports housemates with emotional support and counseling referrals.

Personal belongings are inventoried against the property inventory in the presence of a second staff member and released to the legal representative or other legally authorized person with signed receipt; funds and property are handled under RTS-05.
The Program Director reports the census change to APD within 5 calendar days and notifies the support coordinator so billing and waiver records can be updated under GOV-05.
The Program Director ensures that the death is entered into the quality review and mortality review process under GOV-04 and that findings are reviewed by the Facility Operator.
Staff are offered debriefing and support, and the Program Director reviews staff actions for any needed training or procedural changes.

responsibilities.duty: Call 911, begin CPR, notify the Program Director, protect other residents and preserve the scene.
Make all notifications and APD reports, preserve records, coordinate belongings and census update.
Oversee compliance, cooperate with investigators and ensure mortality review.
Receive immediate notification and coordinate arrangements and waiver updates.

documentation: Incident narrative and daily notes
APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 and notification log with times
Abuse Hotline report number (if applicable)
Preserved record, video footage and medication records
Property inventory and signed receipt of belongings
Census change report to APD
Mortality review documentation

policies.title: First Aid, CPR and Emergency Response Readiness
policies.applies_to: All DSPs, the Program Director and the Facility Operator
policies.purpose: To ensure the home is equipped and staffed to give first aid and CPR immediately, and that staff know the facility's emergency procedures.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps an American Red Cross-approved or equivalent first aid kit on the premises with unexpired contents, in a location known to and readily available to all DSPs, and stores any potentially toxic contents safely. Each DSP completes a basic first aid course, including the abdominal thrust maneuver, and CPR certification within 90 days of providing direct services. Courses must be taught in a classroom by a certified trainer; online or computer-based courses are not acceptable. At least one DSP with current CPR certification is on site whenever residents are present. All staff are knowledgeable of the facility's emergency procedures.

definitions.definition: A kit approved by the American Red Cross or equivalent, with supplies appropriate for the residents and the home.
In-person instruction taught by a certified trainer, with hands-on skills practice; online-only or computer-based courses do not qualify.
A valid, unexpired certification obtained from a classroom course.

procedures: The Program Director obtains an American Red Cross-approved or equivalent first aid kit for the home, placed in a central location known to all DSPs, and for each vehicle used to transport residents where applicable.
The Program Director or designee inspects the kit monthly and after each use, replaces used or expired items, and records the inspection with date and initials.
Any potentially toxic contents of the kit are stored safely and out of the reach of residents who may be at risk of misuse, consistent with each resident's plan.
During orientation, each new DSP is shown the first aid kit location, the emergency numbers and the facility's emergency procedures, and signs an acknowledgment.
Each DSP completes a classroom basic first aid course that includes the abdominal thrust maneuver, and a classroom CPR course, within 90 days of beginning to provide direct services.
The Program Director verifies that each course is classroom-based and taught by a certified trainer, and does not accept online or computer-based courses.
The Program Director keeps a tracking log of each DSP's first aid and CPR dates and expiration dates, and reviews it at least monthly.
The Program Director prepares each weekly schedule so at least one DSP with current CPR certification is on site whenever residents are present, and documents the CPR-certified DSP on the schedule.
If no CPR-certified DSP is available for a shift, the Program Director corrects the schedule before the shift, and does not leave residents without a CPR-certified DSP.
Staff review the facility's emergency procedures, including calling 911, fire response, evacuation and missing resident procedures, at orientation and at least annually, and the review is documented.
Emergency numbers are posted at every phone extension and verified monthly under HLT-04.
The Program Director holds periodic emergency response practice, such as scenarios for choking or medical emergencies, and documents participants and lessons learned.
Training records are kept for at least 3 years under STF-04 and STF-06.
The Facility Operator reviews first aid kit checks, certification tracking and any gaps during quarterly quality reviews under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Equip the home, track certifications, schedule CPR-certified coverage and verify training is classroom-based.
Complete required training on time, know the kit location, and respond to emergencies.
Provide resources for training and supplies and review compliance.

documentation: First aid kit inspection log
First aid and CPR certificates and course provider information
CPR/first aid tracking log with expiration dates
Weekly schedules showing CPR-certified coverage
Orientation acknowledgment of emergency procedures
Emergency procedure review and practice records

policies.title: Specialized and Adaptive Equipment
policies.applies_to: All residents who use specialized or adaptive equipment, DSPs and the Program Director
policies.purpose: To ensure staff can safely apply, monitor, operate and remove each resident's specialized equipment, and that worn or damaged equipment is promptly reported and addressed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] ensures that all DSPs are trained and competent in applying, monitoring and removing specialized equipment worn by residents, such as ankle-foot orthoses (AFOs), braces, splints, neck collars, helmets and safety belts, and are knowledgeable in operating wheelchairs, lifts and positioning devices. When staff notice significant wear and tear on a resident's specialized equipment, they contact the support coordinator as soon as possible.

definitions.definition: Equipment worn by or used for a resident, including AFOs, braces, splints, neck collars, helmets, safety belts, wheelchairs, lifts and positioning devices.
Damage or deterioration that affects the equipment's safety, fit or function.

procedures: At admission and at each plan update, the Program Director lists all specialized and adaptive equipment each resident uses, with the prescriber's or therapist's written instructions for use, schedule, skin checks and cleaning.
The Program Director places the instructions in the resident record and in a location accessible to DSPs.
Before working alone with a resident who uses equipment, each DSP is trained and shown how to apply, monitor and remove it, with a return demonstration by the DSP.
Each DSP is trained on operating wheelchairs, lifts and positioning devices, including brakes, safe transfers and positioning, with a return demonstration.
The Program Director documents each training with date, trainer, content and DSP signature, and retrains staff when a resident's equipment or instructions change.
DSPs apply and remove equipment according to the written schedule and instructions, and check the resident's skin, comfort and fit at the times specified.
DSPs report any skin irritation, redness, pressure marks, pain or fit problems to the Program Director on the same shift, who contacts the physician or therapist as directed under HLT-02.
DSPs inspect each resident's equipment for damage or wear at the start of each shift or at least daily and note concerns on the daily record.
The Program Director performs a documented monthly check of wheelchairs, lifts and other devices, including brakes, tires, belts and batteries, and removes unsafe equipment from use.

When significant wear and tear is noticed, the DSP informs the Program Director immediately and the Program Director contacts the support coordinator as soon as possible, documenting the date, person contacted and the outcome.
The Program Director follows up with the support coordinator, vendor or therapist until repair or replacement is arranged, and documents the date completed.
Staff do not modify or improvise repairs to equipment unless authorized by the prescriber, therapist or vendor.
If equipment failure or misuse causes an injury, staff follow HLT-04 and BSP-04.
The Program Director reviews equipment needs at each plan update and shares information with the support coordinator.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain instructions, train staff, perform monthly checks and contact the support coordinator about wear and tear.
Apply, monitor, operate and remove equipment as trained and report problems promptly.
Assist in arranging repair, replacement or evaluation of equipment.

documentation: Equipment list and written use instructions in the resident record
Staff training and return-demonstration records
Daily equipment checks in the daily record
Monthly equipment inspection log
Support coordinator contact log and repair/replacement records

policies.title: Positive Behavior Support and Behavior Plans
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, all Direct Support Professionals (DSPs), the Waiver Support Coordinator liaison, and contracted behavior analysts serving residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] supports residents with dignity, prevents problematic behavior through positive supports, and implements every behavior plan exactly as written, reviewed and approved, as required by s. 393.13, F.S., Chapters 65G-2, 65G-4 and 65G-8, F.A.C., and the iBudget Waiver Services Coverage and Limitations Handbook.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written statement of policies and procedures governing staff actions to prevent or respond to problematic behaviors, including emergency procedures and reporting, consistent with s. 393.13, F.S. and Chapters 65G-4 and 65G-8, F.A.C. (Rule 65G-2.009(8)(a)). Staff facilitate implementation of each resident's behavior plan and use reactive strategies only as written in that plan (Rule 65G-2.009(1)(a)1-2). No behavioral program is implemented unless it has been reviewed under APD rule (s. 393.13, F.S.). Staff are trained on each resident's behavior plan by a certified behavior analyst, and the training is documented in the personnel record (Rule 65G-2.008(7)(f)). Behavior analysis services plans are submitted to the Local Review Committee (LRC) chair within 5 working days after implementation (Rule 65G-4.010(1)). Any home serving residents under a behavior-focus or intensive behavioral designation holds the required APD designation and meets the monitoring and staff training standards in the iBudget handbook (Rule 59G-13.070, pp. 2-48, 2-52 and 2-53). Behavior support is never used as punishment or for staff convenience.

definitions.definition: A written plan developed by a certified behavior analyst or other qualified professional that identifies target behaviors, proactive and teaching strategies, and, where approved, reactive strategies.
A behavior analyst certified as required under APD rules (for example, a BCBA) who develops, supervises or monitors behavior analysis services.
The APD committee that reviews and approves or disapproves behavior analysis service plans that use restricted procedures.
A planned response used when a person's behavior presents imminent risk of harm and proactive strategies have not been sufficient. Use is governed by Chapter 65G-8, F.A.C. and BSP-02.
An APD-approved designation for Residential Habilitation providers serving individuals with significant behavioral support needs (handbook p. 2-48).

procedures: The Facility Operator/Program Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) makes this policy and the facility's written behavior-response procedures available in the staff area and reviews them with every new DSP at orientation. The review is documented in the personnel record.

Before admission and at each support plan update, the Program Director asks the Waiver Support Coordinator for any current behavior plan, functional assessment, LRC approval and consent documents, and files them in the resident's record (see PCS-01 and PCS-02).

The Program Director confirms that each behavior plan has been developed by, or is supervised by, a certified behavior analyst. The Program Director does not allow staff to implement an unreviewed, unwritten or informal behavior program.

The Program Director confirms with the behavior analyst that the plan was sent to the LRC chair within 5 working days after implementation, and keeps a copy of the transmittal or LRC correspondence in the resident's record.

If the LRC disapproves a plan, the Program Director confirms with the behavior analyst that the plan is revised and resubmitted within 14 working days (Rule 65G-4.008). Staff follow only the last approved version until the revised plan is approved.

Before a DSP implements any resident's behavior plan, a certified behavior analyst trains the DSP on that plan. The Program Director records the date, trainer, trainer credential and topics in the personnel record, and re-trains staff each time the plan is revised.

DSPs use proactive and positive supports first: offering choices, predictable routines, communication supports, meaningful activities, privacy and attention to unmet needs such as pain, hunger, fatigue and boredom.

DSPs implement the plan exactly as written. They do not add, change or improvise consequences, restrictions or physical responses. If a DSP believes a strategy is unsafe or ineffective, the DSP tells the Program Director the same shift.

On each shift, DSPs record behavior data and the supports used, as the plan requires, in the daily documentation (see PCS-03). The Program Director forwards data to the behavior analyst on the schedule the behavior analyst sets.
Reactive strategies are used only if they are written in the approved plan and only by staff who hold current certification in an APD-approved emergency procedure curriculum (see BSP-02).

For any residents served under a behavior-focus or intensive behavioral designation, the Program Director confirms before service starts that APD has granted the designation. The Program Director also confirms that a BCBA or Chapter 490/491 licensee will provide the required face-to-face monitoring (handbook p. 2-52), and keeps the monitoring schedule and notes.

For those residents, the Program Director confirms that each DSP has 20 contact hours in an APD-approved curriculum (or is a Registered Behavior Technician, or has 90 classroom hours of applied behavior analysis), plus APD-approved emergency procedures training, with yearly recertification (handbook pp. 2-52 to 2-53). A training matrix tracks due dates.

The Program Director reports any incident involving a behavior intervention through BSP-04. Any proposed limit on a resident's rights goes through RTS-02 and is never handled as an informal behavior strategy.

The Program Director reviews behavior data and incidents with the behavior analyst at least monthly. The Program Director asks the Support Coordinator for a plan review when data show that the plan is not effective or is no longer needed.

The Program Director includes behavior plan implementation, training currency and LRC status in the quality review (see GOV-04) and reviews this policy at least annually. Because the Chapter 65G-8 and 65G-4 text is under revision, the Program Director confirms the current rule text with APD at each review.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures plans are approved, staff are trained and certified, designations and monitoring are in place, and records are complete.
Implements plans exactly as written, uses positive supports first, records data and reports concerns.
Develops or supervises plans, submits plans to the LRC, trains staff on each plan and monitors implementation.
Coordinates plan updates and informs the team of approvals and changes.

documentation: Current behavior plan, functional assessment and LRC transmittal/approval in the resident's record
Staff behavior plan training records in each personnel record, retained at least 3 years
Shift behavior data and daily documentation
Behavior-focus designation letter, monitoring notes and staff training matrix, where applicable
Monthly behavior review notes

policies.title: Restrictive Interventions, Reactive Strategies, Restraint and Seclusion
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director and all staff of [AGENCY NAME], including relief and contracted staff
federal: 42 CFR 483.450 (applies to ICF/IID only; used here as best practice, not as a legal citation for waiver homes)
policies.purpose: To protect residents from unnecessary restraint, seclusion and harmful practices, and to limit any reactive strategy to certified staff acting under an approved plan in compliance with s. 393.13, F.S., Rule 65G-2.009 and Chapter 65G-8, F.A.C.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to be free from unnecessary restraint and seclusion (s. 393.13, F.S.). Staff may not use any emergency intervention that involves restraint or seclusion, or that causes physical discomfort, unless they are certified through an APD-approved emergency procedure curriculum under Chapter 65G-8, F.A.C. (Rule 65G-2.009(8)(c)). The curriculum requires at least 12 direct training hours and a written test with an 80% minimum score, and certification is valid for one year (Rule 65G-8.002). The following are strictly forbidden: physical or corporal punishment (hitting, slapping, pinching, pulling hair, pushing); noxious substances (pepper on the tongue, ammonia, electric shock); verbal abuse; humiliation (wet or soiled clothing, dunce cap, signs); dark or locked time-out rooms; and any reactive strategy prohibited by Rule 65G-8.009 (Rule 65G-2.009(8)(d)). [AGENCY NAME] provides training on these policies, keeps consent information in the resident's record (Rule 65G-8.003(1)), documents and gives notice as required by Rule 65G-8.010, and conducts an internal review at least annually (Rule 65G-8.003(6)). Chapter 65G-8 as cited is the 2008 adoption, and APD has revisions in development, so [AGENCY NAME] confirms the current text before relying on it.

definitions.definition: Any physical, mechanical or chemical method that restricts a person's freedom of movement, physical activity or normal access to the body. Chemical restraint is addressed in Rule 65G-8.008.
Involuntary confinement of a person alone in a room or area from which the person is physically prevented from leaving.
A planned response to behavior that creates imminent risk of harm, used only as approved under Chapter 65G-8 and the resident's behavior plan.
An APD-approved training program in reactive strategies that meets Rule 65G-8.002 (12 hours minimum, 80% written test, one-year certification).
Any practice listed in Rule 65G-2.009(8)(d) or Rule 65G-8.009, which may never be used under any circumstances.

procedures: [AGENCY NAME] does not use restraint, seclusion or any intervention that causes physical discomfort as routine practice, for punishment, for staff convenience or as a substitute for adequate staffing or supports.

The Program Director identifies, with each resident's behavior analyst, whether any reactive strategy is part of the resident's approved plan. Only strategies that appear in the plan may be used (see BSP-01).

The Program Director enrolls designated staff in an APD-approved emergency procedure curriculum. Before using any technique, staff must have completed at least 12 direct training hours, scored at least 80% on the written test, and received certification.

The Program Director tracks each staff member's certification expiration date (one year from certification) and schedules recertification before it lapses. A staff member whose certification has lapsed may not use any technique until recertified.
The Program Director schedules staff so that, to the extent possible, a certified staff member is on duty whenever a resident with an approved reactive strategy is in the home.
All staff are trained on this policy and the forbidden practices before working alone with residents, and the training is documented in the personnel record.

Staff first use de-escalation, environmental changes, redirection and the proactive strategies in the plan. They apply a reactive strategy only when the plan's criteria for imminent risk are met, and they stop as soon as the risk has ended.

If no certified staff member is present and a resident's behavior creates imminent danger, staff move other residents and themselves to safety, remove hazards where possible, avoid any physical hold, and call 911. Staff then notify the Program Director.
Staff never use a dark or locked room, a locked door or any enclosure to isolate a resident, and never withhold food, water, medication, sleep, personal items or contact with family as a consequence.

Chemical restraint is not used. Any psychotropic medication use follows prescriber orders and consent requirements and is never given to control behavior outside of a prescribed, consented regimen (see HLT-01 and RTS-06).
Immediately after any use of a reactive strategy, staff check the resident and others for injury, obtain medical care as needed (see HLT-04), and tell the Program Director.

Staff complete documentation and notifications required by Rule 65G-8.010 and complete an incident report under BSP-04 before the end of the shift. The Program Director notifies the legal representative and Waiver Support Coordinator and reports to APD within the BSP-04 timeframes.
The Program Director reviews each use of a reactive strategy with the behavior analyst within [NUMBER] business days to determine whether the plan, supports or training need to change.
The Program Director keeps the consent information required by Rule 65G-8.003(1) in each resident's record and confirms it is current.

The Program Director conducts and documents an internal review of reactive strategy use, staff certification and these procedures at least annually (Rule 65G-8.003(6)) and refers findings to the quality review (GOV-04). During that review the Program Director confirms the current text of Chapter 65G-8 with APD.

Any suspected misuse of restraint, seclusion or a prohibited procedure is treated as suspected abuse and reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline under BSP-03. The staff member involved is handled under BSP-06.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures staff certification, scheduling, consent information, post-event review, notifications and the annual internal review.
Use only plan-approved reactive strategies within their training, stop when risk ends, and document the event.
Never use prohibited practices; report suspected misuse immediately.
Specifies approved strategies in the plan and reviews each event with the team.

documentation: Emergency procedure curriculum certificates, test scores and expiration dates in personnel records
Consent information for reactive strategies in the resident's record
Incident reports and Rule 65G-8.010 documentation of each event
Post-event review notes
Annual internal review report
Training records on this policy, retained at least 3 years

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All employees, relief staff, volunteers, contractors and the Facility Operator/Program Director of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To prevent abuse, neglect and exploitation of residents and to make sure every known or suspected case is reported immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline and to the people required to be notified.
policies.policy: Residents have the right to be free from abuse, neglect and exploitation (s. 393.13, F.S. and Rule 65G-2.009(1)(b)1). Any known or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation is reported immediately to the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 under ss. 39.201 and 415.1034, F.S. (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(a)). Reporting to the Hotline comes first. Every DSP completes Zero Tolerance training before providing direct services and a refresher every 3 years, and must demonstrate the reporting procedures in theory and practice (Rule 65G-2.008(7)(c)). The legal representative and support coordinator are notified immediately (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(c)). A DCF verified finding is a critical incident that requires 4-hour notice to APD (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(f)3.i). [AGENCY NAME] cooperates with DCF investigations and requests documentation of the conclusion of each investigation (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(e)). No employee may be retaliated against for reporting in good faith.

definitions.definition: Any act or failure to act that causes or could reasonably cause physical, sexual or emotional harm to a resident, including physical or corporal punishment, verbal abuse and humiliation.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medical care or other services necessary to maintain a resident's health and safety.
Improper use of a resident's funds, property, assets or labor for the benefit of someone other than the resident.
The Department of Children and Families hotline for reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation: 1-800-962-2873.
A DCF investigative conclusion that the alleged abuse, neglect or exploitation is supported by the evidence.
The required training on prevention and reporting of abuse, neglect and exploitation, completed before direct services and refreshed every 3 years.

procedures: The Program Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) ensures that every DSP completes Zero Tolerance training before providing any direct service, including a demonstration of reporting procedures in theory and practice, and documents the completion date in the personnel record.
The Program Director tracks each DSP's refresher due date (every 3 years) and schedules the refresher before it expires.
The Program Director posts the Abuse Hotline number, 1-800-962-2873, near each phone and in the staff area, and gives each resident the number in a format the resident can understand (see RTS-07).

Any staff member who sees, hears of or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation of a resident calls the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately. The staff member does not wait for a supervisor's approval and does not investigate before reporting.
The staff member records the Hotline intake number, date, time and the name of the intake worker.

The staff member immediately protects the resident: ensures safety, separates the resident from any alleged perpetrator, obtains medical care (see HLT-04) and preserves evidence by not cleaning or discarding relevant items.

The staff member notifies the Program Director immediately after making the Hotline report. If the Program Director is the alleged perpetrator, staff notify the [GOVERNING BODY OR OWNER NAME] and the APD Regional Office.
The Program Director immediately notifies the resident's legal representative (guardian, guardian advocate or other representative) and the Waiver Support Coordinator.
The Program Director determines whether the event is also a critical or reportable incident and completes APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 under BSP-04 within the required timeframes.
If the alleged perpetrator is an employee, the Program Director immediately applies BSP-06 so that the person is not alone with residents and has no access to resident funds.
Staff cooperate fully with DCF and law enforcement investigators, provide records and access as requested, and do not discourage residents or witnesses from speaking with investigators.

The Program Director requests written documentation of the conclusion of each investigation from DCF and files it in the appropriate record (resident's record and, where applicable, the personnel record).

On receipt of a DCF verified finding, the Program Director reports it to the APD Regional Office as a critical incident with initial notice within 4 hours of awareness and the completed form within 1 calendar day, then follows BSP-06.

The Program Director reviews each report and its outcome within [NUMBER] business days to identify prevention steps, such as supervision changes, retraining, environmental changes or a revised support plan, and documents the review in the incident file.
The Program Director prohibits retaliation against any person who reports, and reminds staff of this at staff meetings. Retaliation results in discipline up to termination.
The Program Director reviews abuse, neglect and exploitation reports in the quality review (see GOV-04) at least quarterly to identify trends.

responsibilities.duty: Report suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation to the Hotline immediately, protect the resident and notify the Program Director.
Ensures training, posting, notifications, incident reporting, protection of residents, cooperation with investigators and prevention follow-up.
Receives reports that involve the Program Director and supports corrective action.
Receives immediate notification and coordinates follow-up supports.

documentation: Hotline intake number, date and time of report
APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 and Regional Office notices
Notification record for legal representative and support coordinator
Zero Tolerance training certificates in personnel records, retained at least 3 years
DCF investigation conclusion documents
Prevention review notes

policies.title: Reportable Incidents and Investigations
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director and all staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every critical and reportable incident is responded to, reported to APD on the required forms and timelines, investigated and followed up until resolved.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports incidents on APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 (December 2025), submitted electronically to the Regional Office (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(b),(e)). Abuse, neglect and exploitation are reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline first (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(a)). For critical incidents, initial notice is given within 4 hours of awareness by phone, e-mail or APD's designated system, and the completed form is submitted within 1 calendar day. Reportable incidents are submitted within 1 calendar day. Follow-up measures are submitted to the Regional Office within 5 days after the incident is reported, with ongoing follow-up until the incident is resolved (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(h)). Incident reports involving a resident are kept in the resident's record (Rule 65G-2.009(5)(c)8).

definitions.definition: An incident requiring 4-hour initial notice: unexpected death; any sexual activity between a covered person and a resident; absence over 1 hour of a minor or adjudicated-incompetent adult; life-threatening injury or illness; hospitalization from a medication error; negative news media; arrest of a resident for a violent crime; arrest of a covered person for a disqualifying offense; a DCF verified finding; suspected or confirmed human trafficking; and a person left in a vehicle (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(f)).

An incident due within 1 calendar day: a non-unexpected death; physical altercations with law enforcement contact; injury needing urgent care, ER or hospital; non-violent arrest; a competent adult absent over 8 hours; suicide attempt; Baker Act or voluntary commitment; injury to a covered person caused by a resident; and sudden-onset illness needing urgent care or hospital admission (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(g)).
An employee or other person subject to screening and working with residents of the facility.
APD Incident Reporting Form (December 2025) used to report critical and reportable incidents.
Corrective and preventive actions reported to the Regional Office within 5 days after the incident is reported.

procedures: The staff member on duty first protects the safety of all residents, provides first aid or calls 911 as needed (see HLT-04), and secures the scene.

If the incident involves known or suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the staff member calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately, before any other report, and follows BSP-03.
The staff member notifies the Program Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) at [PHONE] immediately. The Program Director is reachable 24 hours a day through [ON-CALL PHONE].

The Program Director determines the same day whether the event is a critical incident, a reportable incident or neither, using the lists in this policy. When in doubt, the Program Director treats the event as the more serious category.

For a critical incident, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours of becoming aware, by phone, e-mail or APD's designated system, and records the time, method and person contacted.
The Program Director submits the completed Form OP 3-0006 electronically to the Regional Office within 1 calendar day of a critical incident.
For a reportable incident, the Program Director submits the completed Form OP 3-0006 to the Regional Office within 1 calendar day.
The Program Director immediately notifies the resident's legal representative and the Waiver Support Coordinator of any incident involving the resident, and documents the contact.

The staff member who witnessed or discovered the incident writes a factual statement before the end of the shift, covering who, what, when, where, injuries and actions taken, and does not alter other staff statements.

The Program Director begins an internal review immediately, collecting statements, daily documentation, schedules, physical evidence, and medical or police records, and cooperates with any DCF or law enforcement investigation.
The Program Director identifies the causes and contributing factors and develops follow-up measures, such as supervision changes, training, plan revisions, repairs or medical follow-up.
The Program Director submits follow-up measures to the Regional Office within 5 days after the incident is reported, and continues to submit updates until the incident is resolved.
If an employee is arrested for a disqualifying offense or is the subject of an allegation, the Program Director takes action under BSP-06 and STF-02 and reports as a critical incident where required.

If media contact occurs, staff refer all inquiries to the Program Director, share no resident information (see RTS-04 and RTS-10), and the Program Director reports negative news media as a critical incident.
The Program Director files a copy of the incident report and follow-up in the resident's record, keeps the incident log current, and reviews all incidents at least quarterly for trends under GOV-04.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure safety, report to the Hotline when required, notify the Program Director immediately and write a statement.
Classifies incidents, meets all APD timelines, notifies representatives, investigates, submits follow-up and maintains the incident log.
Receives notification and coordinates resident support follow-up.
Receives reports and may require additional information or corrective action.

documentation: APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 with submission confirmation
Record of 4-hour critical incident notice (time, method, person)
Staff statements and investigation file
Follow-up measures sent to the Regional Office within 5 days and later updates
Notification records for legal representative and support coordinator
Incident log and copy in the resident's record

policies.title: Missing Person and Elopement
policies.applies_to: All staff and the Facility Operator/Program Director of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure a resident who is missing is located quickly, that law enforcement is engaged immediately, and that required notifications to APD and the resident's representatives are made on time.
policies.policy: After determining that a resident is missing, staff immediately call local law enforcement and ask the officer to take a report, assign a case number and provide it, and give the facility a copy of the report when available (Rule 65G-2.010(5)(a)-(c)). If the officer refuses to take a report, staff document the officer's name, call the law enforcement agency and ask for the Watch Commander (Rule 65G-2.010(5)(d)). A critical incident report is required, with initial notice within 4 hours, when a minor or adjudicated-incompetent adult is missing over 1 hour (Rule 65G-2.010(5)(e); (6)(f)3.c). A legally competent adult missing over 8 hours is a reportable incident due within 1 calendar day (Rule 65G-2.010(6)(g)5). The legal representative and support coordinator are notified immediately. Residents are never left unattended in a vehicle (Rule 65G-2.009(14)(p)).

definitions.definition: A resident whose whereabouts are unknown and who is not where the support plan or schedule says the resident should be.
A resident leaving the home or a supervised setting without the knowledge or permission required by the resident's plan, or in a manner that puts the resident at risk.
An adult who a court has found legally incompetent and for whom a guardian has been appointed.
The supervising officer of a law enforcement agency's shift, contacted if an officer refuses to take a report.
A documented risk that a resident may leave without permission or safe supervision, addressed in the support plan and any safety plan.

procedures: Staff identify each resident's elopement or wandering risk at admission and support plan updates, and the Program Director records the risk, the resident's recent photograph, a physical description and identifying information in an accessible, confidential location (see PCS-01 and PCS-02).

Staff keep residents in line of sight, or within the supervision level in the plan, and conduct a headcount at each activity change, upon return from outings and at each shift change (see STF-01 and PCS-06).

When a resident is not where expected, the staff member immediately checks the house, yard, vehicles, bathrooms and the resident's known preferred places for no more than [NUMBER] minutes. Staff must not delay the next step when risk is high.

After determining the resident is missing, the staff member immediately calls local law enforcement at 911, provides the resident's description, clothing, risks (such as medical needs, inability to recognize danger, or no traffic awareness) and last known location, and asks the officer to take a report.

The staff member asks the officer for the case number and records it, the officer's name and the time of the call. If the officer refuses to take a report, the staff member documents the officer's name, calls the law enforcement agency, asks for the Watch Commander, and documents the outcome.
The staff member keeps other residents supervised, calls additional staff in if needed, and does not leave other residents unattended to search.

The staff member notifies the Program Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) at [PHONE] immediately, and the Program Director immediately notifies the resident's legal representative and the Waiver Support Coordinator.

The Program Director determines whether the resident is a minor or an adjudicated-incompetent adult. If so, and the resident has been absent more than 1 hour, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours as a critical incident and submits Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day (see BSP-04).
If the resident is a legally competent adult who has been absent more than 8 hours, the Program Director submits Form OP 3-0006 as a reportable incident within 1 calendar day.

If circumstances suggest abuse, neglect, exploitation or human trafficking, the Program Director calls the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873 immediately and reports as required under BSP-03 and BSP-04.
Staff stay in contact with law enforcement, share new information immediately and continue to search as directed by law enforcement.

When the resident is found, staff check the resident for injury and health concerns, obtain medical care if needed (see HLT-04), provide comfort and privacy, and tell law enforcement, the Program Director, the legal representative and the support coordinator that the resident has been found.
The Program Director obtains a copy of the law enforcement report when available and files it with the incident report in the resident's record.

The Program Director completes a review within [NUMBER] business days, covering how the event occurred, whether supervision, door safeguards or the support plan need to change, and whether the plan needs a team meeting. Follow-up measures go to the Regional Office within 5 days after the incident is reported (see BSP-04).

Staff never leave a resident unattended in a vehicle (see ENV-06), and staff on outings keep to the supervision ratio in the plan. The Program Director trains all staff on this policy at orientation and at least annually, and conducts a missing-resident drill at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Search briefly, call law enforcement immediately, supervise other residents and notify the Program Director.
Makes APD notifications, informs representatives, obtains the law enforcement report and completes the review.
Receives immediate notification and participates in any plan change.
Takes the report, issues the case number and leads the search.

documentation: Law enforcement case number, officer name and copy of report
Documentation of Watch Commander contact, if the officer refused a report
APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 and 4-hour notice record (if applicable)
Notification record for legal representative and support coordinator
Resident photo and description sheet and elopement risk assessment
Post-event review and follow-up measures

policies.title: Staff Named in Protective Investigations; Verified Findings and Corrective Action Plans
policies.applies_to: Facility Operator/Program Director, supervisors and all employees of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect residents while an employee is the subject of a protective investigation, and to respond to verified findings with a timely Corrective Action Plan, as required by Rule 65G-2.008(5), F.A.C.
policies.policy: A person identified as an alleged perpetrator in an active protective investigation must not be alone with residents or have access to resident funds unless under the constant visual supervision of another worker who is not named in the investigation (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(b)). A verified finding makes the licensee subject to disciplinary action under s. 393.0673, F.S. (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(a)). After a verified finding against a person who remains employed, [AGENCY NAME] submits a Corrective Action Plan to the Regional Office within 15 days of notification of the finding. The plan explains why employment is not terminated, the discipline imposed, the training received (with dates) and how residents will be protected (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(c)). If the investigation closes with no verified finding, unsupervised contact may resume (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(d)). A verified finding by DCF is also a critical incident requiring 4-hour notice. Employees remain subject to Level 2 screening requirements under s. 393.0655, F.S. and STF-02.

definitions.definition: A person identified in a report to the Florida Abuse Hotline as having committed or been responsible for abuse, neglect or exploitation.
An investigation by DCF or law enforcement that has not yet reached a conclusion.
Continuous line-of-sight observation of the named employee by another worker who is not named in the investigation.
A DCF conclusion that the allegation of abuse, neglect or exploitation is supported by the evidence.
A written plan submitted to the Regional Office after a verified finding against a retained employee.

procedures: On learning that an employee is named in a Hotline report or protective investigation (from DCF, the Hotline or any other source), the Program Director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) immediately restricts the employee from being alone with any resident and from handling, accessing or recording resident funds or property.

The Program Director adjusts the schedule the same shift so that the named employee works only under the constant visual supervision of another worker who is not named in the investigation, and documents who is the supervising worker on each shift.

The Program Director tells the named employee in writing, without disclosing confidential details, of the temporary restrictions, that retaliation against reporters is prohibited, and that the employee must cooperate with investigators.

The Program Director confirms that the Hotline report was made and that the legal representative and support coordinator were notified (see BSP-03). If the person is a covered person who was arrested for a disqualifying offense, the Program Director gives critical incident notice under BSP-04 and acts under STF-02.
The Program Director removes the named employee's access to resident funds, keys to funds storage and financial records (see RTS-05), and reviews recent fund transactions with a second staff member.

The Program Director determines whether the employee must be removed from direct service entirely based on severity, resident safety and available supervising staff, and takes that step if safe supervision cannot be provided.
The Program Director cooperates fully with DCF and law enforcement and keeps a log of dates and investigator contacts.
The Program Director requests written documentation of the investigation's conclusion from DCF and files it in the personnel record.

If the investigation closes with no verified finding, the Program Director documents the closure, notifies the employee in writing that restrictions end, and permits unsupervised contact to resume (Rule 65G-2.008(5)(d)).

If DCF issues a verified finding, the Program Director gives initial notice to the APD Regional Office within 4 hours of awareness as a critical incident and submits Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day (see BSP-04).

For a verified finding against an employee who will continue to be employed, the Program Director consults the governing body ([GOVERNING BODY OR OWNER NAME]) within [NUMBER] business days and decides on discipline, retraining and continued employment, with documented reasons.

The Program Director submits the Corrective Action Plan to the Regional Office within 15 days of notification of the verified finding. The plan states why employment is not terminated, the discipline imposed, the training received with dates, and how residents will be protected.

The Program Director ensures the employee completes any retraining named in the plan (for example Zero Tolerance and behavior-support training) before the plan is submitted, and records training dates in the personnel record (see STF-04).

The Program Director continues protective measures, such as supervision or limits on duties, as stated in the Corrective Action Plan, and verifies compliance weekly until [NUMBER] days have passed or the Regional Office approves ending them.
If a verified finding results in termination, the Program Director documents the termination and follows STF-02 and STF-06 for screening and personnel records.
The Program Director reviews each protective investigation and corrective action in the quality review (GOV-04) and reports any APD request for records within the required deadline.

responsibilities.duty: Immediately restricts access, arranges supervision, notifies APD, develops and submits the Corrective Action Plan and monitors compliance.
Maintains constant visual supervision of the named employee and documents it.
Follows restrictions, cooperates with investigators and completes required retraining.
Reviews discipline and employment decisions after a verified finding.

documentation: Written notice of restrictions to the named employee
Schedules and supervision logs showing constant visual supervision
DCF investigation conclusion
APD critical incident notice and Form OP 3-0006 for a verified finding
Corrective Action Plan and proof of submission to the Regional Office within 15 days
Training records, discipline records and monitoring notes in the personnel record

policies.title: Sexual Activity, Personal Boundaries and Safety Plans
policies.applies_to: All owners, the facility operator/program director, direct support professionals (DSPs), nurses, volunteers, contractors and any other person who works in or for [AGENCY NAME], and all residents of the group home
policies.purpose: To protect residents from sexual abuse and exploitation, to preserve each adult resident's civil and legal rights to dignity, privacy and relationships, and to meet the requirement that the licensed group home maintain a written sexual activity policy and Safety Plan safeguards under Rule 65G-2.009, F.A.C.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains and enforces this written sexual activity policy, which is also submitted as an attachment to the license application. The policy (1) explicitly prohibits sexual activity between a resident and any covered person; (2) prohibits sexual activity involving any resident under 18 years of age; and (3) does not abridge the civil and legal rights of persons with developmental disabilities under s. 393.13, F.S. Every DSP is trained on this policy. Residents with a history of sexually aggressive behavior, or who have a Safety Plan, receive the additional safeguards in this policy. Any sexual activity between a covered person and a resident is treated as a critical incident and reported to the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately and to APD within 4 hours.

definitions.definition: A person who works for or on behalf of [AGENCY NAME] or is otherwise covered by the prohibition in Rule 65G-2.009, including owners, the facility operator, employees, volunteers and contractors. If there is doubt whether a person is covered, treat the person as covered and consult the facility operator.
Any sexual contact, sexual conduct or sexually exploitative behavior, including sexual contact that a resident cannot or does not freely consent to.

A written plan, signed by the resident or the resident's representative, that sets out safeguards for a resident with a history of sexually aggressive behavior or other sexual-safety risk. It is reviewed at least annually.
A resident with a documented history of sexual behavior directed at others without consent, or who is identified by APD, the support coordinator or the referral team as presenting that risk.
Staff continuously able to see the resident, so that the resident is never out of sight of a DSP.
An incident requiring an initial notice to APD within 4 hours and the completed APD Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day.

procedures: The facility operator/program director ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) maintains this written policy, ensures it is included in the license application packet, and reviews it at least annually under GOV-03.

The policy states in plain language that sexual activity between a resident and any covered person is prohibited and that sexual activity involving a resident under 18 is prohibited. No exception is allowed.

Each adult resident's rights to privacy, dignity, social interaction and personal relationships under s. 393.13, F.S., are honored. Staff do not impose rules on consensual adult relationships beyond what this policy, the resident's support plan and a documented rights restriction under RTS-02 allow.

Where there is a question about a resident's ability to consent, the facility operator refers the question to the resident's support coordinator, guardian or guardian advocate and the interdisciplinary team under RTS-06. Staff do not decide capacity on their own.
Staff dress code: DSPs wear clothing that is modest, clean and appropriate to a residential care setting. The staff dress code is posted in the staff area and reviewed at orientation.

Personal space: staff knock and wait for a response before entering a resident's bedroom, except where a documented need for visual supervision (for example, a Safety Plan or seizure protocol) requires otherwise. The documented exception is recorded in the resident's support plan.

Bedroom visits: residents may visit another resident's bedroom only as the house rules, the residents' wishes and any Safety Plan allow. House rules state who may visit whose bedroom, and staff apply them consistently.
Beds: each resident and each DSP has a separate bed. No resident shares a bed with another resident or a staff member.

Personal care: DSPs assist with bathing, showering and toileting only as the resident's plan directs and with respect for privacy. A staff member never bathes or toilets at the same time as a resident.

Supervision: staff follow the supervision guidelines in each resident's plan and in STF-01. Staff are never alone with a resident behind a closed bedroom or bathroom door unless the resident's plan permits it for personal care.

Open communication: the facility operator tells residents and staff at orientation and in house meetings that they may report any concern without fear of retaliation. Staff are told whom to call, including the Florida Abuse Hotline at 1-800-962-2873.
Training: all DSPs are trained on this policy during orientation under STF-04 and before working alone with residents. The training date and trainer are recorded in the personnel record.

Pre-admission review: for a prospective resident with a history of sexual aggression or an existing Safety Plan, the facility operator and the DSPs who will work with the resident review the available history. The Safety Plan is reviewed before admission under PCS-01.

Safety Plan training and signature: all staff are trained on the resident's Safety Plan before they work with that resident. The resident or the resident's representative signs the Safety Plan, and a copy is kept in the resident record.
First 24 hours: a newly placed sexually aggressive resident is under visual supervision whenever awake during the first 24 hours after placement.

Bedrooms and closed spaces: a sexually aggressive resident does not share a bedroom with another resident without written APD approval. The resident is never left alone with another person in a bedroom or bathroom behind closed doors without written APD approval.
Safety Plan review: the facility operator reviews each Safety Plan at least annually and whenever the resident's behavior or circumstances change. The review date and any revisions are documented.

Minors: if a resident is under 18, no obscene materials, as defined by Florida law, are allowed in the home. The facility operator checks that the home complies at admission and during monthly environmental checks.

Reporting: if a staff member suspects or learns of sexual activity between a covered person and a resident, or any sexual abuse or exploitation of a resident, the staff member calls the Florida Abuse Hotline immediately and notifies the facility operator. Staff do not wait for facility review before calling.

APD notice: the facility operator gives APD initial notice of the critical incident within 4 hours and submits the completed Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006 within 1 calendar day, with follow-up reporting within 5 days as required under BSP-04. The staff member involved is removed from contact with residents pending the investigation under BSP-06.

responsibilities.duty: Owns this policy; ensures it is included in the license application; ensures training, Safety Plan compliance and annual review; makes reports to APD within the required deadlines; documents all decisions.
Follow the policy; complete training; respect personal space and privacy; follow Safety Plans and supervision guidelines; report concerns immediately.
Advises on health and personal care aspects of supervision and contributes to Safety Plan review.
Receive information about their rights and the policy; sign the Safety Plan where one applies.
Is notified of Safety Plan development and revisions and of reportable incidents; assists in consent questions.

documentation: Written Sexual Activity Policy (copy attached to the license application)
DSP training records on the policy with dates and signatures
Safety Plan, signed by the resident or representative, with annual review dates
Record of pre-admission history review and DSP review before placement
Visual supervision log for the first 24 hours of a newly placed sexually aggressive resident
APD approval for any shared bedroom or closed-door exception
Documented exception for visual supervision needs in the support plan
Incident Reporting Form OP 3-0006, Abuse Hotline report number and follow-up documentation

policies.title: Residential Environment and Accessibility
policies.applies_to: The facility operator/program director, owners, maintenance staff, DSPs and any person responsible for the physical plant of the licensed group home
federal: ADA Title III (28 CFR 36) as applicable
policies.purpose: To make sure the group home's physical plant meets Florida licensing standards and federal home and community-based settings requirements, is safe, is accessible to the people who live there, and is a home, not an institution.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] operates the group home in a site-built home that meets Rule 65G-2.007 and Rule 65G-2.0072, F.A.C. The home has no mobile or manufactured structure, adequate bedroom, bathroom and living space for every household member, safe water temperature, working detection equipment and secured hazards. It has an office area with secure records storage. The home is designed or modified to be accessible to the disabilities of the residents. Residents may decorate and personalize their bedrooms and may use common areas, and any modification of HCBS setting rights is justified and documented under RTS-02.

definitions.definition: Any person who lives in the home, including residents and any staff or operator living in the home, for purposes of space calculations.
A bedroom occupied by two residents, which is the maximum for homes first licensed on or after July 1, 2014.
A licensed home that is subject to local siting and zoning rules under s. 419.001, F.S.
A pool, pond, hot tub or other body of water that could create a risk of drowning.

procedures: Before the home is proposed for licensure, the facility operator confirms that the structure is a site-built home. The agency does not use a mobile or manufactured home.

The facility operator verifies siting before applying: no more than three APD-licensed facilities within 1,000 feet, and the zoning category fits the home's size. Homes of 6 or fewer residents are a single-family use; homes of 7 to 14 residents must be in multifamily zoning, and the local government has 60 days to approve or deny. The result is filed.
When the first resident moves in, the facility operator notifies the local zoning authority in writing and keeps a copy of the notice.

The facility operator measures every bedroom and records the square footage. Single bedrooms are at least 80 square feet. Shared bedrooms provide at least 60 square feet per person. No more than 2 residents share a bedroom (homes first licensed on or after July 1, 2014). The bedroom must open directly onto a common area, and staff-only bedrooms are not counted toward capacity.

The facility operator verifies one toilet, one sink and one tub or shower for every 3 residents, and at least 35 square feet of living and dining space for each household member. The home is ventilated, heated and cooled.
